activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: In England and Wales, a landlord must place a tenant's deposit in a government-backed protection scheme within 30 days of receiving it.
story:
Brooke had planned to be in and out of the bank in ten minutes: deposit her graduation money, ask one question at the counter, and be home before her mother noticed the envelope of cash had left the drawer. Instead she was still in line at the branch on Marsh Street, watching an old man argue with a teller about a mortgage payment, when her phone buzzed with a message from Cory.

"Is it normal that I never got any paperwork about my deposit?" he wrote. "Like nothing. Paid it in April."

Cory had spent the year in England on an exchange, and instead of student housing he had rented a room in a landlord's terraced house in a town whose name Brooke could never remember how to pronounce. She had visited him once in March, riding three buses, and had been enraptured by the place in a way that embarrassed her now: the narrow stairs, the kettle, the window that opened onto someone else's garden. The landlord, a broad man named nothing she'd caught, had taken Cory's money in cash and written him a receipt on the back of an envelope. Brooke had watched that and said nothing, because it wasn't her deposit, wasn't her country, wasn't her business.

She typed back "let me ask" and then stood there composing a second message she didn't send, because the truth was she had no idea. In school, Ms. Perera had taught them the vocabulary of money the way she taught everything, briskly and without sentiment: deposits, interest, the difference between renting and owning. Brooke had liked the unit on mortgages, had even done the reading twice, because numbers behaved, unlike most of what had happened that spring. She understood that a down payment was a chunk of money paid up front, that the mortgage covered the rest, and that the bank held the house like a promise until you paid it off. Rent was simpler and somehow sadder: money that left and never came back, month after month, like water through an open hand.

Her turn came. She slid the envelope under the glass, watched the teller count, and then, feeling foolish, asked the question she'd come with. "If someone wanted to save for a down payment, is there a better account than this one?" The teller, young, with a lanyard and tired eyes, said the bank had a savings account with a slightly better rate and a limit on withdrawals, and that honestly, for most people her age, the important thing was not the rate but the habit. Brooke opened the account because it was something to do, and because Ms. Perera had once said that a bank account was a record of who you were deciding to be. Then, since the teller had been kind, she took a chance. "Sorry, random question. If a landlord takes a deposit from a tenant in England, does the tenant get anything for it? Like paperwork?"

The teller frowned. "I wouldn't know, love. Different country, different rules." But a man behind her in the queue, grey jumper, canvas bag, leaned in and said, "My daughter rents in Manchester. There's a scheme. The landlord has to put your deposit in a government-backed protection scheme within 30 days of getting it. That's the law in England and Wales."

Brooke thanked him, stepped to the side near the leaflets, and texted Cory the whole thing, word for word as she could manage: deposit, protection scheme, government-backed, 30 days. She could picture him on the other end, in that narrow room, holding his phone and doing the arithmetic on a landlord who had done none. His reply took four minutes. "So he owes me the paperwork? He never said anything about any scheme."

"You never got anything," she wrote. "So no, not normal."

"It's only four hundred pounds," he wrote next, and then, a moment later, "or I could just not make trouble. I leave in June anyway."

There it was, the thing Brooke recognised from her own life, the small wrong you could walk past because walking was easier and the door was already open behind you. She thought of her new savings account, twenty minutes old, the first honest step toward a down payment on a place that would take her a decade to afford, if ever. She thought of how the pernicious part of money trouble was never the sum itself but the silence people kept around it, the way not knowing protected the person who already had the power. She had spent a year learning the rules for herself, hoarding them, and Cory had spent a year not knowing the rules that protected him.

"Ask him for it in writing," she texted. "You don't have to be angry. Just ask what scheme it's in." She added, "Worst case you learn something. Best case you get four hundred pounds back."

He sent a thumbs up, then a message that said "I'll do it tomorrow," which she knew from long experience meant maybe. Then: "how was the bank?"

She looked around before answering. The old man with the mortgage had finally reached an arrangement with the teller and was signing something slowly, pressing hard, as though the paper might argue with him. The man in the grey jumper was now at the counter, depositing a stack of envelopes with the ease of someone who had done it a thousand times. Outside, the light was going the flat gold of late afternoon, and she could see the bus stop, and beyond it the street where Kailey's flat was, the one with the broken intercom that Brooke had helped pay to fix because they all pretended it was theirs.

"Opened a savings account," she wrote. "I'm going to own something someday. Probably something small."

"Phylogeny of your money," Cory replied, which made no sense until she worked out he'd been revising biology all afternoon and meant the family tree of it, the line of descent from envelope to account to whatever came next. She laughed out loud, alone, near the leaflets, and a woman glanced over.

Cory's next message arrived while she was still smiling: "Landlord just texted me asking if I want to renew for next year." Below it, a second one, a full minute later, "He says he's 'happy to keep the arrangement as it is.'"

Brooke stood in the bank with her phone warm in her hand, thumb hovering, deciding what to tell him.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: An off-book rehearsal is one where actors must perform without their scripts, having memorised their lines.
story:
Sophia had taped a floor plan of the stage to her bedroom carpet, the living room rearranged into a rehearsal space, and by seven o'clock on Thursday the coffee table was the kitchen counter of the play's set. Tucker leaned against the doorway eating cereal from a mug while Sukhman sat cross-legged on the rug, script open on her knees, highlighter bleeding through the pages. Sophia stood at the edge of her taped rectangle holding a pencil in each hand like a tiny traffic controller.

"Places," she said. "We open in four days and tonight we go off-book."

Sukhman stood up and set her script on the couch, face down. Tucker kept chewing.

"Off-book," he said, "as in..."

"As in we perform without scripts. Lines memorised. Mr. Sutherland set the date, not me." She said it evenly, though she had spent the walk home from school rehearsing how to say it evenly, because Tucker had been her friend since grade eight and she had watched him talk his way through three group projects on charm alone.

Tucker set the mug on the mantel and picked up his script anyway, holding it low, the way a kid holds a security blanket at arm's length and pretends it isn't there. "I've been busy. Immunology unit, my mom's working nights, I had the car." He ran the excuse like a line, with feeling, and Sophia realised with a small cold drop in her stomach that he had learned the words to everything except the play.

She started the scene anyway. Sukhman moved through her blocking cleanly, crossing downstage of the coffee table on her cue, and her voice filled the room the way it filled the school auditorium. Tucker made it through his first two lines. On the third he stopped, looked at the ceiling as if the line had been stored there, and said, "Can I just, one sec," and reached for the script he had sworn he didn't need.

"No," Sophia said. She heard how hard the word came out and softened the next one. "Try it wrong. Anything. Move."

He moved. He improvised something that was not the line but had the shape of it, and Sukhman, God bless her, played it straight, and the scene kept breathing. Then it happened again, and again, and by the fourth silence Sukhman was staring at Sophia with the particular look of someone who has done her part and is waiting for someone else's problem to be solved. The radiator ticked. Somewhere upstairs a television murmured through the floor.

Mr. Sutherland had told them, the whole directing class, that the schedule was sacred. "Theatre runs on deadlines," he had said, tapping the rehearsal calendar with two fingers. "If you move the date, the date will move you." Sophia had written it in her notebook and underlined it, because she liked rules that held still. But she had also watched her mother, a nurse, come home at midnight all through her childhood and still make breakfast, and she knew that people carrying heavy things sometimes need a door held open rather than a bell rung in their faces. She had never had to decide which of those beliefs she actually held until now, standing in her own living room with four days left.

"Five minute break," she said. Tucker retreated to the kitchen, and she heard him whispering lines to himself over the running tap, sublimating his panic into the sound of water, as if the script could be rinsed into him. Sukhman came and stood beside her at the taped edge of the stage.

"You can't move the off-book date," Sukhman said quietly. "The performance is Saturday whether he's ready or not."

"I know." Sophia looked at the floor plan, the little arrows she had drawn for every crossing, and she understood that blocking was the one thing she could give Tucker that didn't require him to have the words. "I'm not moving it. I'm changing what we do with the time we have."

When Tucker came back, drying his hands on his jeans, she had dragged the coffee table to a new position. "New plan," she said. "We run the physical scene ten times, no lines at all. You talk through it, paraphrase, hum, I don't care. Your body learns where it goes. Then, tonight, last half hour, we do lines sitting down, just voices." She handed him the pencil from behind her ear. "And every time you move without me telling you, you check the line on your own before Friday."

"That's backwards," Tucker said. "Isn't it?"

"It's how the words catch up to the feet. Or it isn't, and we find out by ten o'clock."

They ran it. Tucker bumped the coffee table twice, then once, then not at all, and somewhere in the sixth repetition he said a full line, the real one, out of nowhere, as if the movement had carried it up from somewhere somatic, below thinking. Sukhman laughed out loud, surprised, and Sophia wrote the number six on the back of her hand. They still had three and a half scenes of words he didn't own, and Friday loomed like a held breath, but when Tucker asked, "Again?", she was already moving back to her mark.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Doubling the size of a sorted list adds only one extra step to a binary search, while it doubles the worst-case work of a linear search.
story:
The robotics lab at Camp Wenlock smelled of solder and sunscreen, and by Tuesday of the second week Jessica had claimed the corner workstation with the good monitor. The team's parts inventory lived in a text file on the camp server, sorted by part number, and Mr. Zhou had sequestered it behind a login so nobody could reorder seventeen servo motors by accident again. That morning Ava arrived holding her tablet like a verdict.

"Inventory doubled overnight," Ava said. "Mr. Zhou merged in the returned parts from the session before ours. Four hundred lines now, was two hundred." She dropped into the folding chair beside Jessica. "So we should probably switch the lookup to the slow table method everyone warned us about?"

Jessica didn't answer right away. The team had two functions in their code: one walked the list from the top, comparing each part number in turn, and the other kept cutting the list in half by checking the middle entry first. Annabelle had written the first one back when the file held only two hundred lines, and it had seemed fine then, quick enough that nobody questioned it.

They ran both. On the old two-hundred-line file, Annabelle's function took a number of steps Jessica wrote on the whiteboard, and the halving function took seven. On the new four-hundred-line file, Annabelle's function roughly doubled its work, grinding through a worst case that made the test on the terminal visibly slower, while the halving function came back in eight steps. One extra step. Jessica circled it.

"That can't be right," Annabelle said, leaning over her shoulder. "The list is twice as big. Everything's twice as slow when things are twice as big. That's just physics."

"It's not physics," Jessica said. "It's arithmetic on sorted things." She wasn't entirely sure she could say why, only that the numbers on the whiteboard said so, and she was honest enough with herself to admit the gap between those two kinds of knowing. She had grown up with her father insisting that anything true should be provable on paper, and her mother, a museum conservator, insisting that some true things could only be shown, layer by layer, the way she read sedimentary rock faces in the field photos on her desk at home. Two habits of mind Jessica had never managed to reconcile, and which now both seemed to want a turn.

She got the laptop and walked to the window bay where Mr. Zhou was untangling a spool of wire.

"Mr. Zhou," she said, "the halving function, the binary search, it only got one step slower when the list doubled. Annabelle's function doubled its work. Is that real, or is something broken?"

Mr. Zhou looked at the whiteboard, then at her, and gave her the particular flat smile he used when he was declining to rescue anyone. "What does the whiteboard say?"

"It says one step."

"Then propose it at standup," he said, and turned back to his wire.

At standup, in the hot half hour before lunch, Jessica stood up with the whiteboard behind her. She explained that the binary search beat the linear search on sorted data, and that she trusted it because she had watched the two functions diverge on a real file, not because she could derive it. Annabelle argued back, twice, and twice Jessica pointed at the circled eight. She said the doubling claim held for the worst case, and that she hadn't tested enough runs to speak to averages, and that if Annabelle wanted, they could instrument the timer after lunch. Ava asked whether it mattered, since two hundred or four hundred lines both came back in under a second anyway, and Jessica conceded the point, which surprised her more than the whiteboard had.

They instrumented the timer anyway. Annabelle wrote the patch, Ava picked test part numbers at random, and Jessica ran the file with its four hundred sorted entries while the fan on the old camp laptop rattled and someone outside called a soccer score through the window. When the last run finished, Annabelle stood looking at the numbers for a long moment, then picked up the marker and crossed out her old estimate on the whiteboard without a word.

"Fine," she said. "Binary search stays in. But you're writing the comment block."

Jessica took the marker and wrote at the top of the function, "This is called binary search," and under it, in smaller letters, "It beats linear search on sorted data."

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: Payment history is the largest factor in a FICO credit score, making up about 35 percent of it for the general population.
story:
The line at the credit union moved in small, patient shuffles, and Noah stood behind Jesse with a folded printout going soft in his hand. The printout was his problem, or rather the problem was the ninety-three dollars he'd owed a phone company since March, sitting on the paper like a splinter. He had forgotten the bill entirely, then paid it the week a collections letter arrived, and now he wanted to know what kind of scar it had left.

"You could just apply and see," Jesse said, nodding at the loan officer's desk near the window. "They tell you the rate, and if it's terrible, you know."

"That's like checking if the ice is thin by walking on it."

Jesse shrugged. His family had a laconic way of handling money, if handling was the word; his father paid cash for everything, even a car once, sliding bills across a table like a poker player. Noah's mother did the opposite, financing a washing machine over three years, and when he'd asked her why, she said the interest made it cost more than the sticker, but not by much, and she'd said it the way you describe weather. He had never thought to ask how much more, exactly, until this spring, when the number stopped being abstract.

Dana was already at the counter, opening her first savings account before college. Noah watched the teller slide a rate sheet toward her, watched Dana bend over it, her finger moving down a column. He caught the phrase "compounded monthly" drifting back through the lobby's fluorescent quiet, and something about the phrase snagged him. Money sitting still, growing by itself. It was the same mechanism that made his mother's washing machine cost more, only pointed the other way, running in reverse like a river made to flow uphill.

"Next," the loan officer said. She was younger than he expected, maybe thirty, with a jar of pens that looked requisitioned from a supply closet three decades ago.

"I want to know about a small loan," Noah said, sitting. "Like two thousand dollars. For a laptop before school starts. But mostly I want to know what my credit looks like."

She turned her monitor toward him, and there it was: a number with his name above it, smaller than he'd hoped, and a stack of colored bars beneath it like a chart of his carelessness rendered in red and orange.

"Is that because of the phone bill?" he asked. "It went to collections but I paid it."

"The score's made of a few things," she said, and clicked to a diagram shaped like a pie. "Payment history is the biggest one. About thirty-five percent, for the general population." She said it flatly, the way a mechanic names a part, and moved the cursor on.

Thirty-five percent. More than a third of the whole number riding on whether he remembered to pay things. He sat with that for a second. It seemed both harsh and, strangely, fair; if a stranger wanted to know whether you could be trusted with borrowed money, wasn't the first question whether you'd paid people back before? The system wasn't punishing his character, only his record, and his record had one bad spring in it.

"So if I take the loan and pay it perfectly, the history part gets better."

"It can," she said. "Nothing's guaranteed. Collections entries fade in weight over time."

He asked her to run the numbers on the loan anyway. At the rate his score bought him, two thousand dollars became about twenty-two hundred over three years; he wrote the figure in the margin of his printout. Then he made her do the reverse, the same two thousand parked in savings at Dana's rate, compounding monthly, and watched it swell past twenty-one hundred over the same three years. Not equal, but close enough that the shape of the thing was visible: borrowed money grew heavier in your hands, saved money grew heavier in the vault, and the difference between the two lives was small decisions made on time.

He found Dana still filling out forms at the counter, Jesse reading the pamphlet rack with the concentration of a man studying rival religions.

"Do you know what a confounder is?" Dana asked, apropos of nothing, which was her way. "From stats. It's a hidden thing that affects both variables and makes you think one caused the other. Like, people who carry lighters get more cancer, but it's the cigarettes."

"Why are you telling me this?"

"Because you're about to take a loan to fix your credit, and I can't tell if that's smart or if you just like the idea of the pie chart improving. Your plan is fixing the thing and also the thing it measures. That could be a confounder."

Noah laughed, then stopped, because she might be right. Maybe paying a loan perfectly and having a good score were so tangled that no one could say which pulled which. He couldn't resolve it standing there, and the honest position, he decided, was to act anyway on the part he did understand: interest was real, thirty-five percent was real, and both directions of the river existed.

He walked back to the desk and signed the application. The loan officer stamped it and told him the first payment date, and he entered it into his phone before the paper had left his hand, then set an alarm for three days earlier.

"Two alarms," Dana said, reading over his shoulder.

"Both banks of the river," he said, and pocketed the phone.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: Niger has one of the highest birth rates in the world, so its population pyramid has a very wide base and a large share of children.
story:
Aiden told Lucie he had already finished the geography assignment, which was true in the sense that he had opened the textbook, looked at the diagrams, and closed it again. He had told Andrew the same thing in the bus queue, and Andrew had believed him, because Aiden was the kind of student who usually did finish things first. That was the version of himself he preferred to narrate, and he narrated it often. Now it was Thursday evening, the assignment was due Monday, and the public library smelled of radiator dust and someone's microwaved soup. He spread the atlas across two tables near the geography shelf and began, at last, to look.

Lucie found him there twenty minutes later, coat still on, holding a printout of her own. "I thought you were done," she said.

"I'm revising."

She sat down anyway, which was generous of her, though Aiden did not put it that way even to himself. She slid her printout across: four population pyramids, one per country, each a pair of back-to-back bars showing ages up the side and numbers of males and females across the bottom. Japan's looked like a top spinning on a wide point, narrow at the bottom, bulging in the middle years. Niger's looked like something else entirely, a steep triangle, wide at the base and tapering fast.

"That one's broken," Aiden said.

"It's not broken. Mr. Sow gave us that one on purpose."

Aiden leaned closer. The bottom bars, the zero to four age group, stretched so far sideways they nearly left the page. He counted the segments with his pen tip, tapping each one, and the tapping slowed as he went up the pyramid and the bars shrank. The whole shape was children. He had assumed every country would look roughly like a rectangle with a rounded top, because that was what a country was, people of all ages, and he had not thought past it. "So half the country is under some ridiculous age," he said.

"You're the one who supposedly finished." Lucie pulled the textbook toward her and found the country table. Niger had one of the highest birth rates in the world, which was why the base was so wide and why such a large share of the population was children. She read it aloud, flat, like a train announcement, and Aiden wrote it down without arguing, because the fact and the picture agreed with each other and he could see the agreement in front of him.

Mr. Sow passed their table on his way to the returns desk, carrying a stack of atlases with his chin steadying the top one. He stopped. "Which one have you got there?" Aiden showed him the triangle, and Mr. Sow nodded once. "Tell me on Monday whether Niger needs more schools or more nursing homes. Use the shape, not the name."

Lucie turned her page to Japan, with its narrow base and its fat middle, and Aiden set the two printouts side by side. Japan would be building homes and wards for its old; that was obvious from the bulge. Niger was the opposite problem, and the answer was not abstract, it was a certain number of classrooms, teachers, desks, chalkboards, all of it implied by the width of that lowest bar. And yet Aiden kept snagging on something he could not resolve aloud: a wide base did not tell you whether the classrooms existed or whether the country was too destitute to build them, and the pyramid, for all its clarity, kept its mouth shut about money. He said some of this to Lucie, half of it, editing as he went, and she said, "So put that in the answer. Say what it shows and what it doesn't." He was quiet for a moment, because admitting an unfinished thought was not the character he had been narrating all week.

Andrew arrived at closing time, famished, complaining that the vending machine had eaten his coins and that he was in no mood to be a gourmand on crisps alone. He dropped into the chair beside Lucie and looked at the two pyramids without touching them. "Which one's ours due on?"

"Monday. And I didn't finish early," Aiden said. "I prevaricated. For four days."

Andrew looked at him. "You what?"

"I lied. Politely." Aiden gathered the printouts, squared them against the table edge, and slid them into his folder with the Niger triangle facing up, wide base first, the whole country balanced on its youngest people. "Tomorrow I'm coming back at open. You want the table by the window?"

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Mexico's Day of the Dead is traditionally celebrated on November 1 and 2, when families build ofrendas, or home altars, with photos and the favorite foods and drinks of relatives who have died.
story:
The bakery box sat on Luke's knees in the passenger seat, warming his thighs through his jeans. His mother drove with both hands on the wheel, saying nothing, and behind them his father followed in the grandfather's truck with the rest of the boxes. They were driving to the old house to sort the first layer of things, the kitchen first, because the kitchen was easiest. Luke peeled back a corner of the box flap and looked at the pan dulce, conchas with their sugared shells cracked along the ridges, still faintly sweet-smelling. His grandmother had bought them every Sunday for as long as he could remember, and he had bought this last tray this morning without deciding to, the way you catch a ball thrown at you without thinking.

"Mr. Zhang said something yesterday," Luke said. "About November." His mother glanced over. "He teaches world civ, and he's Mexican-American, and he said his family still does it. Day of the Dead. November 1 and 2. They build ofrendas, home altars, with photos of relatives who died, and their favorite foods and drinks, the actual foods, laid out on them." He turned the box on his knees. "He said his mother puts out tequila for an uncle who drank it and hot chocolate for an aunt who didn't drink anything else."

His mother was quiet through one red light and half of another. "We're not Mexican," she said, which Luke understood was not the same as no.

"I know that," he said. "I know it's not ours. But she's not going to have a funeral until December because of the scheduling at the church, and I just keep thinking there's nothing. Nothing anywhere is happening for her right now. Nobody's saying her name anywhere except us."

His mother's jaw worked the way it did when she was deciding whether a thing was grief or an idea, and whether both could be allowed. "What would you even put on it," she said, and he opened the box because that was the answer, or the beginning of one.

In the kitchen, dust hung in the light from the window over the sink and the fridge hummed the same note it had hummed for thirty years. His father brought boxes up from the truck and left them by the door, not opening them, and Luke cleared the small table where his grandmother had kept her mail and her rosary and a bowl of keys that fit nothing anymore. He set the conchas on a plate in the middle. His mother found the photograph in the drawer by the stove, the one from the beach trip where his grandmother was laughing so hard the camera had caught her mid-tilt, half a second from tipping off the log she sat on. She held it a long time before she set it against the wall above the plate.

His father stood in the doorway with his hands in his pockets. "This the thing from Mexico," he said, not a question, and Luke felt the room go careful. "The altar thing."

"Ofrenda," Luke said.

His father crossed the kitchen and looked at the plate and the photograph for a while. "She liked those," he said finally. "The pink ones. She'd eat the shell off first and leave the bread part for last, like a kid." He went to the box, took out one pink concha, and set it apart from the others, closer to the photograph, deliberate as a man placing a stone.

Later Reece texted, and Bruce texted, both asking if he was okay, both offering to come by, and Luke sat on the porch steps answering them while the light went amber over the yard his grandmother had planted. Reece said the altar thing sounded cool and asked if it was like a shrine, which wasn't quite it, and Bruce said his family just did casseroles after funerals, which was its own version of the same need, and Luke understood suddenly that every custom was an encapsulation of the same want, dressed differently, and that saying one was correct and another wasn't was tautological, the custom justifying itself by being itself. He had almost written a reply arguing this when he stopped, because it felt like something he was doing to sound wise at a moment that wasn't about him.

He went back inside. His mother had found the instant coffee, which his grandmother drank by the quart, and set the mug beside the plate without comment. His father had turned the photograph a few degrees so it faced the doorway instead of the window. Luke stood with them, the three of them eating conchas at the table where the ofrenda was, shells first, bread last, the way she had done it, none of them certain whether this was borrowing or inventing or just a family in a kitchen refusing to let a Sunday pass unmarked. His mother broke a piece of the pink one and handed it to his father, who ate it looking at the photograph.

"Same time tomorrow," his father said.

Luke nodded and reached for another concha.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: A blood pressure reading gives two numbers in millimeters of mercury: systolic pressure when the heart beats, over diastolic pressure when the heart relaxes between beats.
story:
The camp brochure had promised "hands-on health science," and Ms. Bakker, who ran the program, took the promise seriously enough to load eleven teenagers into a van on the second Wednesday and drive them to the pharmacy in town. Olivia sat between Cayden and Camilla, the permission slip folded into her pocket, and watched the trees give way to a strip mall. She had signed up for the session because her mother wanted her to be interested in something, and because nursing paid well, and because the scholarship the camp offered was munificent enough that refusing it would have felt ungrateful. None of those were reasons, exactly. They were more like a chronology of excuses, one following another until she was on the bus in June with a duffel bag and a notebook she had promised herself she would actually use.

The pharmacy had one of those machines near the pharmacy counter, a molded chair with a cuff built into the armrest, free to anyone who sat down. Ms. Bakker gave them a single instruction before letting them loose: find something in the store they could not explain, and explain it by Friday. Olivia wrote the assignment in her notebook, transcribing it word for word the way she did with anything that might later be used against her, and then Cayden said the machine and she felt the idea settle before she had decided anything.

Camilla went first, because Camilla always went first. She slid her arm into the cuff, pressed the button, and sat very still while the cuff tightened and then released with a hiss. The screen showed a fraction. "What does that even mean," she said. "It looks like math."

Cayden leaned over her shoulder. "One-twenty over, um, seventy-eight." He took a picture of it with his phone, as though the number would not be there when he looked again.

"It's two numbers," Olivia said slowly, and then stopped, because she did not actually know what the two numbers were, only that everyone said them that way, over, like a fraction that never got simplified. She had heard her grandfather's doctor recite them at every appointment, and she had never asked. She wrote "120/78" in her notebook and then, underneath, "top? bottom?" and hated how it looked.

It was Camilla's grandmother who settled it, without meaning to. She had driven in from the next town to take Camilla to dinner, and she had drifted toward the machine while waiting, reading the little laminated card beside it. "My nurse says mine's high, top number," she said to no one in particular. "Says the systolic's the one when the heart beats."

"And the bottom one's diastolic," Olivia said, because she remembered that much from somewhere, a pamphlet in a waiting room, the summer her grandfather's appointments became monthly. "That's when the heart relaxes between beats." She heard the words come out and realized she was not guessing. The two numbers had been sitting in her for a year, unretrieved, and the machine had shaken them loose.

Camilla's grandmother lowered herself into the chair and let the cuff do its work, and while it tightened she talked about the dietitian she was apparently supposed to be seeing, and the walking group at the community center she kept meaning to join. "Salt," she said. "Everyone says salt." Cayden asked whether exercise actually moved the numbers or just made you feel like it did, and the grandmother laughed and said her doctor claimed both, though she had never tested it herself, and Camilla said, half embarrassed, "Grandma, you're supposed to be walking already," and the grandmother said, "I'm supposed to be doing a great many things."

Olivia stood a little apart, watching the screen fill in again, and thought about her grandfather, who had cut the salt shaker from the table like a man removing a witness and had still ended up with two more prescriptions by spring. She had believed, then, that if he had tried harder the numbers would have obeyed him. She was less sure now. Maybe diet and exercise moved the readings and maybe they only moved them sometimes, and a person could do everything right and still carry a number that frightened her mother. She could hold both of those ideas at once, she found, though they rubbed against each other like the two sides of the cuff.

On the ride back she filled two pages, drawing the fraction and labeling each number, writing "beats" and "relaxes" in her smallest hand. Ms. Bakker looked over from the driver's seat at a red light. "Found your Friday topic?" she asked. Olivia said maybe, and it was the truest thing she had said all day, because she still did not know what she believed about the numbers, only that she finally knew what they were called. Camilla's grandmother waved from the parking lot as the van pulled out, one hand raised, the other holding the folded slip of paper the machine had printed for her.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During China's Qingming Festival, which falls on April 4, 5 or 6, families visit their ancestors' graves to sweep and clean them and leave offerings of food.
story:
The hospital corridor smelled of floor wax and something faintly floral, the kind of cleaner they use in places where people are supposed to be getting better. Eli had been standing outside room 412 for a long time, long enough that a nurse with atruculent set to her jaw asked him twice whether he was going in or not. His grandfather had died at four in the morning. It was now almost noon, and Eli had not yet gone in.

"He's still there," his mother had said, which struck Eli as a strange sentence, because of course he wasn't. The body was there. His grandfather, who had taught him to solder wires and to identify wasps by the shape of their nests, was somewhere else or nowhere, and Eli did not know which of those was worse to think about.

He went in. The bed had been tidied, the tubes removed, his grandfather's hands folded on the blanket like they were holding something invisible. Eli sat down and, out of habit, began sorting what he knew. His grandfather had been an entomologist, the kind who could name the genus of any beetle within seconds and who considered sloppy classification a moral failing. It was from him that Eli had learned to want everything named. A thing with a name was a thing you could hold.

Wassim had texted him three times that morning and Eli had answered none of them, so it was no surprise when Wassim appeared at the end of the corridor around one o'clock, still in his delivery jacket, a paper bag of food in his hand that he clearly didn't know what to do with. "My mom sent soup," Wassim said. "She sent it before I told her it was over already."

"Thanks." Eli took the bag so his friend would stop holding it like an offering he was ashamed of.

They sat in the visitors' lounge, where a television mounted near the ceiling played weather with the sound off. Eli told him about the morning, the phone ringing in the dark, the drive in which his mother had said almost nothing and he had been grateful. Wassim listened the way he listened in physics class, completely still, and then he said, "It's bad timing, this week. My family's doing Qingming on Saturday."

Eli said he didn't know what that was.

"My grandfather's grave. We go every spring. It falls on April fourth, fifth or sixth, one of those days, and families visit their ancestors' graves. You sweep and clean them. Leave food." Wassim turned the soup lid over in his hands. "My dad's been going since he was a kid. I used to think it was a chore. Like yard work for dead people."

Eli laughed, a short sound that surprised him, and then stopped laughing because it hadn't been funny, it had been a door. He remembered being eight, in his grandfather's garden, being handed a small broom and told to sweep the flagstone path before they laid out the pit trap for ground beetles. "Cleanliness is data," his grandfather had said, entirely serious, crouching there in his stained field hat. "A messy ground tells you nothing. Sweep, and then whatever you find, you know it came today." Eli had swept that path like it mattered, and the eleven beetles they caught that afternoon had mattered, had been counted and logged and released.

"I used to think that was just him being fussy," Eli said now. "But it wasn't. Sweeping was how you paid attention. Like it was how you said this ground, this day, counts." He looked at the muted television, the little sun icons marching across it. He was circling something and he knew it. "And your family does that at graves."

"Yeah. And the food, it's not like we think he eats it. My dad says it's a meal you have together anyway. He talks to the headstone. Tells him who failed their exams." Wassim shrugged. "I hated it when I was little because it was long and boring and my grandmother cried. Now I don't know. It's the one day a year everybody shows up."

Eli thought about the room down the hall, about his grandfather's hands folded on nothing. There would be a funeral, his mother had said, something at the funeral home with flowers and a minister his grandfather had never met, over in forty minutes. Eli had been assuming that was the shape of it, the one correct ceremony, and that afterward you were supposed to be finished, and what he hated most about the morning was the way he kept feeling he was doing grief wrong, that there was some procedure he'd missed. He wanted to expiate something, though he couldn't have said what; the guilt had no crime attached to it, only the ordinary one of not having visited enough, of having let three weekends go by.

But sitting here it occurred to him that his grandfather, of all people, would have looked at a single ceremony and called it bad science. One observation. No repetition, no method, no checking whether anything was actually communicated. Whereas Wassim's family ran the experiment every spring, same days, fourth or fifth or sixth of April, same grave, same sweeping, and whether or not anything crossed over, the living showed up and the ground was clean and the dead were fed. Maybe that was all any of it was for. Maybe you didn't get certainty. Maybe you got a practice.

"So you're going Saturday," Eli said.

"I'm going Saturday. My dad already asked if you want to come."

"He asked?"

"He said, and I quote, the boy with the beetle grandfather should see it." Wassim stood, zipping his jacket. "I told him I'd ask. So I'm asking."

Eli looked down the corridor toward 412. Later there would be forms, and relatives arriving with casseroles, and his mother needing him to be useful. But Saturday existed, and it had a date, and there were things you could do with your hands. "Tell him yes," Eli said. "Tell him I'll bring the broom."

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: A linear search checks items one by one from the start, so in the worst case, when the target is last or missing, it must look at every item.
story:
Morgan had come to her grandfather's house for the quiet, or so she kept telling herself on the drive up, and not because Krista had beaten her to the working demo two projects in a row. She spread her laptop, the textbook, and a cold mug of the coffee she had sworn off on the kitchen table, under the light fixture with the vestigial pull chain that no longer turned anything on. The house smelled of cedar and last winter's woodsmoke. Her grandfather was in the garden pulling onions, so she had the table to herself.

The program she had promised Krista was simple. A file of nine thousand sorted names, and a box where you typed one, and an answer about whether it was there. Krista's version, built first, typed the name into the file's front end and walked. It started at the top and checked each name against the target, one after another, down the whole list. Morgan had watched it run at midnight in a group chat, timing herself against nothing but her own irritation.

The trouble had surfaced on Thursday. Type a name that exists and the answer came back in a blink. Type a name that is not in the file at all and the box hung, cursor pulsing, for a full three seconds. Krista called it a fluke. Chelsey called it the computer being old. Morgan privately called it something she intended to fix before Monday, which was not the same as admitting she was competitive, because she was not competitive, and she said so twice on the drive.

She typed a missing name and watched the debug counter climb. Nine thousand. It had looked at every single one. Then she typed a name at the very bottom of the file, the last line, and the counter climbed again, all the way up, before the answer appeared. But a name near the top answered almost instantly. She sat back. The program slowed to a crawl exactly when the target was last or missing, because in those cases it had no choice but to look at every item, plodding from the start. It had never been the computer being old. She wrote that in her notes and underlined it, twice.

Her grandfather came in with onions and dirt on his knuckles and asked what had her frowning at a screen on a Saturday. She told him, and started explaining the one-by-one walk, and he did not wait for the end of it. He went to the shelf by the phone, took down the fat dictionary nobody used anymore, and set it in front of her. "Find me molybdenum," he said, and walked back out with the onions. He was like that. He would hand you a thing and leave you alone with it, which Morgan had always found unsentimental, though she caught herself smiling at the closed door.

She did not flip from A. Her thumb went straight to the middle, where M would be, which she then realized she had been doing her whole life without once thinking about it. The middle told her which half to throw away. She threw half away, halved what remained, halved it again. Four opens of the dictionary, five, and molybdenum sat there in grey type as if it had been waiting. Then she tried a word she made up, melborogang, and confirmed it was absent in five opens instead of nine hundred pages. Something that old book was good for, it turned out, was teaching her that her own program had been reading the dictionary like a first-grader.

She typed the new version. Keep a low index and a high index around the whole sorted file, look at the middle name, throw away half, repeat. If the middle name was past the target alphabetically, the half above it died; if before, the half below. She typed a missing name and the counter stopped at fourteen. Fourteen, out of nine thousand. She typed the last name in the file. Fourteen again. She sat very still for a moment, the way she did when a thing worked, and heard the fridge tick and a wasp investigate the window screen.

There was one thing she could not settle. The file had to be sorted or the whole method collapsed; on an unsorted list the old plodding walk was the only honest option. Krista's data was sorted today, but the assignment said nothing about tomorrow's, and Morgan could not make herself pretend that the choice between the two searches was really a choice. She thought about what to say when Krista asked, as Krista would, whether Morgan thought she was so clever. Metacognition, the textbook called it, thinking about your own thinking, and Morgan was aware she was doing a lot of it for someone who wasn't competitive.

She texted Krista a screenshot of the counter at fourteen and one line: "worst case is a missing name, ask me why." Then, because the light was going amber on the garden and her grandfather was back among the onions, she carried the dictionary to the porch steps and opened it at random, somewhere in the middle of everything. From the garden he called, "Found it?" and she called back, "In four tries," and turned another page.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: Behavioral interview questions, such as 'Tell me about a time when...', are built on the idea that past behavior is a good predictor of future behavior.
story:
The interview was on Thursday, and Robert had come to his grandfather's house on Tuesday because it was the only place with a kitchen table nobody else used. He spread the printout of sample questions across the wood, weighted the corners with the sugar bowl and a jar of horseradish, and read the first one aloud. "Tell me about a time when you had to deal with a difficult customer." He had never had a customer. He had never had a job. He read it again, as though repetition might conjure an answer.

Finnley arrived at four with a bag of chips and the confidence of someone whose sister had worked at the garden centre for two summers. "You look at them the whole time," Finnley said, dropping into the chair across the table. "Not, like, staring, but you don't look down when you answer. My sister says that's the first thing they notice." Robert tried it, holding Finnley's gaze while reciting his name and his availability, and discovered that his eyes wanted to escape toward the window, where his grandfather was deadheading roses with kitchen scissors.

They worked through the questions one by one. Where do you see yourself in two years. What are your strengths. Robert answered these fine, in a voice that surprised him with its steadiness. Then Finnley read the next one. "Tell me about a time when you worked on a team and someone wasn't pulling their weight."

"I don't have times," Robert said. "I have school. That's all I have."

"So use school."

"It's not the same thing."

Finnley leaned back and crunched a chip with what seemed like deliberate slowness. "Then you'll sit there and say nothing, and they'll move on to the next kid."

The argument that followed was brief and tectonic in a small way, two positions grinding against each other without either giving way. Robert remonstrated that a group project about the water cycle in grade eleven could not honestly be presented as work experience, that the whole exercise was a kind of laundering, dressing up one kind of thing to look like another. Finnley said it wasn't lying, it was answering the question they actually asked, and if Robert couldn't see the difference that was his problem. Neither of them conceded. Finnley left the last handful of chips on the table and went out to see what Robert's grandfather was doing to the roses.

Ms. Joshi lived next door, and she came over at six with a bowl of tomatoes from her garden, as she did most evenings in August. She found Robert still at the table, still staring at the question. He explained the situation without looking up, partly to her and partly to the printout. "I have no job history, so I have nothing to tell them about."

Ms. Joshi set the bowl down and read the question over his shoulder. "Those are behavioral interview questions," she said. "All the 'tell me about a time when' ones. Past behavior is a good predictor of future behavior, that's the idea they're built on." She wiped her hands on her shorts. "So they don't care where the time happened. School counts. Anything counts, as long as it's true."

Robert sat with that. Past behavior as a predictor. It reframed the whole afternoon, not as laundering but as translation, and yet something in him still resisted the ease of it, the way a rule like that could make any true story into evidence for anything. He asked Finnley about it the next morning, on the porch, and Finnley shrugged. "It's not deep. You did a thing, you'll probably do it again. That's all they mean."

"I keep thinking about the kids who are good at this," Robert said. "The ones who've been rehearsing since they were fifteen. There's a version of me that becomes a sycophant in that chair, tells them whatever shape of answer they want, and gets the job because of it."

"Or there's a version of you that tells them about the water cycle project and gets it because Hubert left you with the whole poster and you finished it anyway."

Robert laughed despite himself, because that was true, that was exactly what had happened, Hubert vanishing for a week and returning the night before it was due, and Robert staying up with the markers and the rolled paper spread across this same table. He had never thought of that night as an answer to anything. It had just been a bad week that ended.

On Thursday he sat across from a woman in a green polo shirt in the back office of the hardware store, and she asked about his availability, and his strengths, and then she folded her hands and said, "Tell me about a time when you had to handle a problem on your own." Robert kept his eyes on hers. Somewhere behind him a till rang, and he began with the poster, with the week, with the night before it was due, and he watched her write something down as he spoke.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: At a Seder, a piece of the middle matzah called the afikoman is set aside, often hidden for children to find, and eaten as the last food of the meal.
story:
The folding chairs at the community hall smelled of lemon polish and decades of spilled punch, and Taylor arranged them in a horseshoe the way her grandmother had once described, one chair for each family that would come to the practice Seder on Sunday. Ms. Otieno, who had offered the hall and her old Haggadot, watched from the kitchen doorway while Taylor counted place settings twice. Taylor was sixteen and had volunteered for this before she fully understood what it involved: leading the whole ceremony, start to finish, for a room of families who mostly knew more than she did. That was the point, her mother had said. Learn it in your hands, not just your head.

Alessandra arrived with a crate of grape juice and a shoebox of candles she had begged from three different shops. She wanted this evening to be perfect too, though for a different reason; her family had never hosted anything at the hall, and she had told Taylor, twice on the walk over, that if the practice went well maybe her father would let them help with the real one next month. She set the candles in a straight line and adjusted each one so the wicks faced the same direction, as if symmetry were a form of insurance.

Between them, Taylor and Alessandra worked through the order of the evening. There were the blessings, the four questions, the story itself, which Taylor feared becoming prolix if she lost her place, since the oldest Haggadah in Ms. Otieno's crate went on for pages about bricks and pharaohs. Ms. Otieno demonstrated breaking the stack of three matzot in half and wrapping the larger half of the middle matzah in a napkin. "The afikoman," she said, holding it up, and Taylor wrote the word in her notebook with a small star beside it. It would be hidden for the children to find, and it had to be eaten as the last food of the meal, after everything else was cleared away.

From Alessandra's side of the room, the evening looked like a machine with one fragile part. She watched Taylor practice the blessings alone in the corner, whispering, stumbling, correcting herself, and she began to understand that the whole ceremony balanced on her friend's memory and nobody else's. Ms. Otieno had drifted out to the parking lot to greet an early arrival. The afikoman sat wrapped in its napkin on the table by the window, unhidden, and Alessandra could not stop glancing at it, the way you glance at a kettle you're not sure you turned off.

Halfway through the run-through, with ten families seated and the youngest children already squirming, Ms. Otieno came back inside, went pale, and whispered to Taylor that she had meant to hide the afikoman an hour ago and had completely forgotten. The meal could not finish without it. Taylor felt her heart palpitate, a quick knocking under her ribs, and for a second the room seemed to hold still around the gefilte fish.

She thought of her grandmother's way, which was precision, everything in its appointed minute, and of her mother's way, which was to say that a tradition you can't bend a little might break instead. Were those really opposites, or just two hands holding the same thing? She didn't know, and there was no time to decide, so she did both. She asked Ms. Otieno to keep the adults occupied with the second cup of wine, then pulled Alessandra behind the stage curtain. "Take this," Taylor whispered, pressing the napkin bundle into her friend's hands, "and hide it somewhere hard but findable. Not the kitchen, the little kids can't go in there."

Alessandra ran the options through her mind like a list of doors. Under the piano was too obvious; taped inside the recycling bin felt like a disincentive, a trick so discouraging the searchers would give up and the ceremony would stall forever. She chose the shelf behind the lost-and-found box, at the height of a chair climbed by a determined nine-year-old, and she was back in her seat before the third blessing ended, breathing hard and grinning.

Later, after the meal, when the children had torn the hall apart and a small boy named by nobody but everyone cheered as Yossi held the recovered bundle above his head, Taylor unwrapped the afikoman and broke it into pieces small enough to go around. Each person ate a fragment, and then nothing more was served, and the evening was over in the right order after all. Alessandra's father, stacking chairs afterward, said to Ms. Otieno that his family would like to help next month, and Alessandra carried the empty crate to the car with her chin lifted.

On the walk home, Taylor's notebook sat heavy in her bag, the starred word on its page, and she turned the evening over like a stone in her pocket, wondering which parts had worked because she had planned them and which had worked because they hadn't gone to plan. She could not separate them, and she found she didn't much want to. A streetlight came on ahead of her, and she quickened her step.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Circumlocution, describing a word you cannot remember instead of stopping, is a recognized communication strategy that keeps a second-language speaker talking.
story:
The clock above the whiteboard gave Sarah four minutes until her turn, and every one of them belonged to Riley, who was already at the front of the room sketching shapes in the air with both hands. Their Spanish class had been reorganized for the spring as a debate seminar, and Ms. Ortiz had drawn the topic out of a mug that morning: whether the city should raise the tax on gasoline to pay for bus lanes. Sarah had argued things before, in English, in civics class, loudly and well. Here she had to do it for five minutes in a language she had been speaking for two years, and the gap between those two versions of herself felt like a hallway with no floor.

She sat in the back row with her outline face-down on the desk. She had written it in Spanish and then, in a smaller hand, translated the hard words in the margins: subsidy, revenue, emissions. She knew that Ms. Ortiz would take the paper away when Sarah stood up, because the whole point of the exercise was to see what survived without the net. Riley was demonstrating that survival was possible. He had forgotten the word for "highway" halfway through and had simply said, in Spanish, "the long road where cars go fast, the one that crosses the city," and kept talking, and nobody had laughed. Sarah had watched the class nod along, and something in her chest had loosened and tightened at the same time.

Jaidyn leaned over from the next seat. "Did you see that?" she whispered, in English, which was against the rules but which Ms. Ortiz pretended not to hear during the watching part of class. "He just talked around it. There's a word for that. Circumlocution. It's like a real strategy, not cheating. My cousin does it at her restaurant job all the time." Sarah nodded and wrote the word in the margin of her outline, under "revenue," and then the clock ran out and Ms. Ortiz held out her hand for the paper.

Standing, Sarah was surprised by how much Spanish arrived at first. She had her opening memorized in the honest sense, the sense where it lived in her mouth rather than on the page, and she laid out the case for the tax: fewer cars, cleaner air for the neighborhoods beside the freeway, money for buses that ran late. She could feel the argument wanting to move faster than her vocabulary, the way a river wants to move faster than its bed, and she slowed her sentences deliberately, choosing the stones she could actually step on.

Then she reached the part about the money, the part that was supposed to be the strong center of her case, and the word was gone. She needed "tax" and there was only a white space where it had been. Her first instinct was to stop, to look at Ms. Ortiz, to ask in English and take the penalty. Instead she heard Riley again, the long road where cars go fast, and she reached for the same door. "The money that people pay to the government," she said in Spanish, "the extra amount, when you buy gasoline, that goes to the city," and Ms. Ortiz's pen, which had been hovering, went back to writing. The class was still with her. Sarah kept going.

Something changed in the keeping. Because she could not say "the tax should rise by three percent," she had to say what rising meant, whom it touched, what it bought, and the argument came out slower and more concrete, like she was building the bridge out of the planks she was standing on. She had planned to end cerebral and strong, with a line about the common good; instead she ended with the woman who sold tamales outside the school, whose commute would cost more but whose son's asthma might cost less, and she did not know whether the arithmetic worked out for that family, and she said so, in Spanish, haltingly: "I don't know if it balances. I believe it does. I can't prove it."

"Tiempo," Ms. Ortiz said, at five minutes exactly, and Sarah sat down with her ears ringing.

Riley turned around and held up his fist, and Jaidyn wrote something in her notebook and slid it across: "You forgot the word and it didn't matter. Better than it mattering." Ms. Ortiz was writing on the rubric, and Sarah could not read it from there, could not tell whether the columns of her own performance adumbrated success or its opposite; she only knew that the tamales sentence, the true one, the unprovable one, was the part the class had leaned into, and that the same slowness that had saved her had eaten her conclusion whole. There was no time to find out which of those weighed more. The bell rang, and Ms. Ortiz said, "Sarah, hang back a second," and turned the rubric toward her.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Psychologist Bruce Tuckman proposed in 1965 that groups develop through four stages: forming, storming, norming and performing.
story:
The Chargers had lost six games in a row, and Laura had stopped counting the errors and started counting the arguments. In the third inning of the Sunday doubleheader, Jessie bobbled a ball at second and Kim yelled from the mound, loud enough for the bleachers to hear, that if Jessie was going to stand there she should at least face the batter. Jessie yelled back. Their shortstop, a junior named only in the scorebook, stood between them with her glove hanging open like she'd forgotten what it was for.

The coach pulled Kim after the fourth inning. Laura was on the bench icing her elbow, close enough to hear him say it, tired and flat, like he was reading a grocery list. "A psychologist named Bruce Tuckman proposed in 1965 that groups develop through four stages. Forming, storming, norming and performing." He snapped the lineup card against his knee. "We're in storming. It's normal." Then he walked off toward the fence, and Kim sat down beside Laura and said nothing for a full minute.

Laura turned the words over while the other team batted around. Forming, she understood; that was the first week of June, when everyone was polite and Kim had actually asked Jessie how her exams went. Storming she understood better than she wanted to. It was the rest of it she couldn't see from here, the idea that after the fighting came anything other than more fighting.

She tried it out on the bus home, sitting across the aisle from Kim, whose headphones were around her neck and not on, which Laura took as permission. "Do you buy it? That the fighting is a stage?" Kim looked out the window at the strip mall going by. "I think Jessie dogged it on that ball." "That's not what I asked." Kim pulled one earbud back on, then, before sealing herself off, said, "I don't know. Maybe." It was more than Laura had gotten out of her in two weeks.

The problem was that Kim wasn't wrong about the ball, and Jessie wasn't wrong about being yelled at, and both of them were too obdurate to say the second thing out loud. Laura had watched Jessie hold her tongue all season, and she'd watched Kim sharpen hers, and somewhere in there she'd habituated to the silence between them, let it become the temperature of the team. She didn't like thinking of herself as someone who let things go, but the evidence was eleven games long.

On Tuesday, Jessie was absent with a dentist appointment, and Laura found herself guarding second base alone during infield drills. She did the pivot a dozen times, and each time she reached for the throw she imagined Kim's glove, and she realized she'd been throwing to where Jessie should have been, not where she was. She had been covering for a fight instead of covering the bag. Mr. Popal, who taught psychology at the high school and kept score for the team in a lawn chair by the backstop, looked up when she swore quietly at herself. "Something, Laura?" "Nothing. Footwork." He went back to his card, and she went back to the bag.

She asked him about it anyway, after drills, while he packed his chair. "Tuckman. Four stages, right? Did he say how you get from storming to the next one?" Mr. Popal folded the chair's legs in, unhurried. "He gave them names. The getting there is your problem." He carried the chair to his car and drove off, which was less like advice and more like homework.

So on Thursday, when Kim cut off Jessie's relay throw in practice and opened her mouth to say something about it, Laura was already moving. She stepped between them, took the ball out of her glove, and held it up. "Norming," she said. "That's the third one. After storming." Jessie blinked. Kim said, "What?" "You heard the coach. Sunday. Forming, storming, norming, performing. 1965, some psychologist. We're supposed to be getting to the third one." Kim's jaw was set, and Laura could feel her own pulse in her wrist where she gripped the ball. Jessie, quietly, said, "You want me at normal depth on that relay?" Kim didn't answer for a long moment. Then she said, "Two steps deeper, the runner at first is fast," and jogged back to the mound.

It wasn't a truce, exactly. Laura couldn't have said whether the idea was true or whether naming a stage was just a way of asking people to pretend, and she thought about that all through batting practice, turning it over the way she turned the ball in her glove. But on the last relay of the afternoon, Jessie took it at normal depth, spun, and threw, and Kim's glove closed around it with a sound like a door shutting firmly on an empty room. Laura stood at the edge of the infield with dirt on her knee and her heart going hard, watching them reset for the next one.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: On a stage in the round, the audience sits on all sides, so the director must keep actors moving so no section only sees their backs.
story:
The problem was the room. Jake had blocked his one-act for the school's proscenium stage, every entrance measured from imaginary wings, every pause pitched toward an audience that sat in one dark mass in front of him. Then Ms. Luo announced that the drama festival had outgrown the theatre, and the one-acts would be performed in the round. His would be staged in his grandfather's living room, a wide pine-floored space with tall windows, because the school's annex smelled of varnish and the auditorium was double-booked.

On Saturday morning Jake arrived to find his grandfather had already dragged the furniture to the walls. "You said you needed emptiness," the old man said, wiping his hands on a rag, and then he went to the kitchen and left Jake alone with the space, which was somehow bigger and smaller than the stage he had imagined.

Danielle came first, script rolled in her fist, then Sahil, who had bicycled across town and stood dripping sweat in the doorway. "So where do we stand?" Sahil asked, and Jake realized he did not know. He had rehearsed them in the classroom with desks pushed back, facing one way, and the blocking had seemed finished. Now he set out his grandfather's kitchen chairs in a ring, ten chairs on the north wall, ten on the south, a few on the east where the windows let in the light.

They ran the opening scene. Danielle crossed to the window to deliver her monologue, the one about her character's father, the one Jake loved best, and Sahil answered her from the armchair Jake had kept as a prop. Halfway through, Jake walked out of the ring and sat in a chair behind the action, and what he saw was ten minutes of Danielle's back and Sahil's profile, two actors aimed at a window as though the play had an audience of sparrows.

"Stop," he said. He walked the circle slowly, the way his grandfather walked the fence line after storms, checking for damage. "If the chairs are on all four sides, somebody is always behind us. Somebody always gets our backs." Sahil spun a chair around and straddled it. "So we can't just stand and talk. We have to keep moving, and turning. Like a slow top."

That was the discovery, and it cost him the afternoon. The blocking he had polished for weeks, the stilled and careful composition he had been proud of, would have to be broken open. Every long exchange now needed a reason to travel: Danielle fetching water, Sahil following her, both of them orbiting the centre of the room so that each wall of chairs got its turn at their faces. It was harder for the actors. Danielle lost her stillness at the window and with it, she said, some of the feeling, and Jake had to find her a new anchor, a slow turn through her monologue that she could grow into.

He made mistakes he could not cauterize out of the script no matter how he cut. In the second scene, Sahil's character gives a speech about the town council and the man who had bullied his way onto it, a speech Jake had written after a unit on demagogues in history class, and in the round it fell apart twice because Sahil kept squaring his shoulders to the south chairs and freezing. "Walk it," Jake said finally. "Make the speech a circle. Work the room like he would." Sahil tried it, prowling the ring, and the speech found a shape it had never had, though Jake noticed, sitting in the north chairs, that the words landed differently depending on where you sat. There was no single best seat anymore, no place from which the play was whole. Every audience would get a partial play, and that, he thought, was either a flaw in the room or the truest thing about it, and he could not decide which.

His grandfather brought in tea at four o'clock, set the tray down, and stayed to watch from the doorway, arms folded. When they finished the run, the old man said only, "Good use of the floor," and went to fetch the biscuits. It was more praise than he gave most things.

The cost was still there on Sunday, when they ran it again. Danielle's monologue was better in the new turning shape, but quieter, the stillness spent to buy movement, and Jake could not get both back at once. He kept the turning. He stood in the centre of the ring after the others had gone, in the long light through his grandfather's windows, and walked the circle himself, slowly, counting chair rows on every side, making sure no section of the room would only see their backs, and behind him his grandfather turned a page of his newspaper and did not look up.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: In The Catcher in the Rye, published in 1951, the narrator Holden Caulfield tells readers, 'I'm the most terrific liar you ever saw in your life.'
story:
The library closed at nine, and the English exam was at eight the next morning, which gave Alice roughly eleven hours to decide whether she believed a single word Holden Caulfield said. She spread the novel on the table between her notes and Kiran's laptop, where Kiran was building a timeline of the plot as if the plot were the problem. It wasn't the plot. Alice had read the book twice and still couldn't tell how much of it she was supposed to trust, and the exam would ask exactly that.

"You're overcomplicating it," Kiran said. "He narrates it, so it happened. Unreliable narrator means he's biased, not inventing."

"That's not what unreliable means." Elsa arrived carrying three coffees and dropped into the chair beside Alice. "It means the telling and the told don't match up. Like when my brother describes any argument he's had."

Alice flipped pages, hunting the passage she'd flagged with a torn corner of her chemistry homework. She found it and put her finger under the line, because she wanted them to see she hadn't made it up. In the novel, published in 1951, the narrator Holden Caulfield tells readers, "I'm the most terrific liar you ever saw in your life." She read it out loud. Kiran stopped typing.

"Wait," Kiran said. "He says that? Flat out?"

"Flat out. Early on. And then he keeps telling you things."

Elsa leaned over the table and stole Alice's highlighter. "So how much of the story do we believe after he admits he lies?"

"That's the exam question," Alice said. "That's literally going to be the exam question."

They worked through it scene by scene, Kiran grudgingly playing the skeptic, Elsa arguing that Holden lied about the small things, the bravado, the fights he claimed to have won, and that the small lies might be exactly why the big confessions, the ones about his brother and his exhaustion, felt true. The obstreperous kid in the story, the one who picked fights with roommates and got knocked down, kept coming up. Alice wrote in the margin: the boasting is unreliable; the fatigue might not be. Then she crossed out "might" and wrote "is," then crossed that out too.

At seven, Elsa's phone buzzed and she held up a hand for quiet. She read a message from Mr. Pelletier, forwarded from the class page, and passed the phone across the table so Alice could read it herself. It said that the exam would include one passage they had not studied in class, unidentified, and that they should be prepared to discuss who was speaking, to whom, and why that mattered. Alice read it twice. "To whom," she said. "He's telling the story to us. To a reader. That's the part I keep skipping."

She pulled a fresh sheet toward her and drafted an answer she'd been circling all evening. If Holden addresses you directly and then confesses to lying, he's not just telling a story, he's negotiating with you, handing you a reason to doubt him and then asking for trust anyway. She tried a sentence about how the reader gets sensitized to every claim, how you start weighing each one, and it nearly worked until she reread it and heard Mr. Pelletier's voice asking her what evidence she had. She crossed out the sentence. Kiran said, "Write that doubt is part of the design, not a flaw in it," and she said, "I can't write what I can't prove."

"You could write what you can't prove," Elsa said. "It's called an essay."

"Everything's called an essay. That's not evidence."

Kiran checked the time. The library would empty soon, and there was a bus at eight forty. Alice kept writing anyway, trying to bring the two views together: on one side, Holden's confession made him the least trustworthy narrator she'd ever met; on the other, a liar who tells you he lies is doing something a liar wouldn't normally do, opening the books on himself. She wrote half a paragraph about the reader standing inside his version of events, seeing the world only as he saw it, the whole story sealed inside his head, no way out and no outside view to check it against. She considered whether to use the word phenomenology, which she'd found in a college essay online, and decided she didn't fully understand it, so she left it out and wrote the idea in her own words instead. That honesty cost her a line she liked. She kept the crossed-out draft visible in the margin, unresolved.

The overhead lights dimmed once, the librarian's warning. Elsa gathered the cups while Kiran packed the laptop, and Alice copied out the final sentence she had: that she believed Holden's exhaustion and not his courage, and that she couldn't yet say why the distinction held, only that it did. She underlined nothing. Elsa read over her shoulder on the way to the door and said, "He'd hate that sentence."

"Good," Alice said, and shoved the book into her bag.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Supercompensation is the idea that the body gets fitter during recovery after training, when it rebuilds beyond its previous level, not during the workout itself.
story:
Joshua had been running the park loop every single day for three weeks, and he was getting slower. He knew this because Jason had timed him, twice, with the stopwatch on his phone, and the second time was worse by eleven seconds. Jason had held the phone up like evidence in a trial.

"That's not how it's supposed to work," Joshua said. They were sitting on the rail by the water fountain, the one that sprayed sideways whenever anyone pressed the button. "You train more, you get faster. That's the whole deal."

"Maybe you're doing it wrong," Jason said. "Or maybe you're, like, broken."

Kaydence arrived then, dropping her bag on the grass, and she had a folder with her, which was never a good sign. She was doing her senior project on training theory and had been trying to get the two of them to care about it for a month. She opened the folder on the rail between them, and there was a graph, hand-drawn, with a line that dipped and then rose higher than it started.

"The workout is the dip," she said, tapping it with her pen. "The body gets fitter during recovery after training, when it rebuilds beyond its previous level. Not during the workout itself."

"So rest is the part that counts," Joshua said slowly.

"It's called supercompensation," Kaydence said, and capped her pen like she was finished with the whole subject.

Joshua looked at the graph. He had been treating rest like a betrayal, like something weak people did on Sundays. His legs had been aching in a flat, permanent way, and he had been proud of it. He thought of his uncle, who polished the old car every weekend, burnishing the same paint until there was barely any paint left.
