He was quiet long enough that Jason poked him. "He's having a crisis."

"I'm planning," Joshua said.

On Monday he showed up at the park with a notebook, and Kaydence, who had clearly decided she was his coach now, looked it over with an expression he would describe as generously neutral. The plan had hard days and easy days and two full rest days, which felt like typos. It had warm-ups, which felt like an insult. She was not effusive about it. She said "this is fine" in the tone of someone grading a passable essay, and Joshua found, to his surprise, that he preferred that. Jason, by contrast, told him it was brilliant and genius and incredible, and Joshua trusted none of it. A sycophant with a stopwatch is still a sycophant, he thought, though he didn't say so, because Jason would look the word up and be wounded.

The first rest day, Tuesday, he walked to the park anyway and sat on the rail doing nothing, which was harder than running. An old man doing tai chi near the willows kept glancing at him like he was a lost dog. Joshua read his plan four times. Rest, it said. He rested, badly.

Friday was the first hard day after proper recovery, and the loop felt different under his feet, the gravel giving back instead of dragging. He ran the hill by the picnic tables twice, which was in the plan, and stopped exactly where the plan said to stop, even though he wanted a third. Ms. Pelletier, who lived in the brick house facing the park and walked her terrier there every evening, paused at the fence.

"You're the boy who used to run himself into the ground daily," she said. "You've developed a certain smugness in your posture."

"It's a training program," he said. "It has rest days."

"Good," she said. "The dog approves." The terrier did not appear to approve of anything, but he took it as a compliment anyway.

The following week Jason timed him again. The first lap was fine. The second lap, the one that always fell apart, held together, and he crossed the line four seconds faster than his best from three weeks ago, back when he was training twice as much. He put his hands on his knees and breathed while Jason squinted at the phone to check he hadn't lied about the math.

"So it works," Jason said.

"It worked once," Joshua said. He didn't want to say more than that. He thought of the graph and its tidy little line, and he thought of his legs, which still ached sometimes, in ways the graph didn't cover. Maybe the rest days were the right amount. Maybe they were too many and he was being soft. Maybe the warm-ups were ritual or maybe they were the whole engine, and he honestly could not tell which parts of the plan were doing the work.

"Same time next week?" Jason said.

"Check the notebook," Joshua said, and pointed at Tuesday, which said, in his own handwriting, REST, with nothing under it yet.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Making ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen is exothermic, so low temperatures favour more ammonia at equilibrium, but industrial plants run hotter because the reaction is too slow when cold.
story:
The garage smelled of WD-40 and old coffee, which Payton decided was the smell of ambition. Mario had claimed it as his future workshop, though the only car in it was his mother's minivan with a flat tire and the only tools were a jack, a torque wrench, and a poster of a Lamborghini he had taped to the wall at age eleven. He had invited the study group there because, he said, genius requires space. Dhruv had come for the pizza. Payton had come because Ms. Morningstar's exam was on Monday and she was still getting the equilibrium questions backwards.

She spread her notes on an upturned milk crate. "Okay. Le Chatelier. The system pushes back when you squeeze it. Heat it, and it shifts to soak up the heat. Cool it, and it shifts the other way."

"Like my ex," Mario said, from under the minivan. "Push, push back."

"You've never had a girlfriend," Dhruv said, shaking the pizza box to redistribute the last slice.

"I'm indigent in love," Mario said with dignity. "It's a condition. Keep reading."

Payton flipped to the practice problem. Nitrogen plus hydrogen going to ammonia, exothermic. She wrote the arrows, drew her little energy hill, and felt the small click of getting something right: cold should favour more ammonia, because the reaction gives off heat, and cooling it is like pulling product away. She wrote "low temp, more ammonia" and underlined it twice.

Dhruv leaned over, chewing. "Then explain this." He held up his phone, a photo of a textbook page. "It says industrial ammonia plants run at a hotter temperature. Four hundred, five hundred degrees. Why would a factory pick the temperature that makes less product? That's like ordering a small fries because you like fries."

Payton looked at the page. Then at her underlined answer, which was still right, and at his page, which was also right, and something in her brain made the noise of two gears finding each other. "Wait," she said slowly. "The equilibrium is one thing. How fast you get there is another thing."

"Meaning what?"

"Meaning if you run it cold, the mixture eventually has more ammonia in it. Eventually. But the reaction is too slow when it's cold, so eventually is basically never. The plant runs hotter even though the equilibrium is worse, because the speed is better. You get less each pass, but you get it this week." She tapped the page. "It's not choosing less product. It's choosing any product."

Mario rolled out from under the van to look at them, a smear of grease across one eyebrow like a doubtful comma. "So it's like a toll road. The cold route gets you more pizza, but it takes eleven hours. The hot route gets you most of a pizza now."

"That's not the metaphor I'd predicate a whole chemistry grade on," Payton said, "but yes."

"I want my own shop by thirty," Mario announced, lying back down. "That's why the garage. Every good mechanic starts with a garage. Tell me that's not true."

"It's mostly true," Dhruv allowed, because Mario's mother had said something about the tire and Mario had been insufferable about it ever since.

Payton turned back to the problem, and here she slowed down, because the click wasn't the whole of it. She understood the two ideas separately and now together, but there was a seam she couldn't iron flat. Somewhere between them the plant operators had picked a number, a temperature, some compromise she couldn't calculate, and she didn't know how they chose it. How much speed was worth how much product. Whether there was a right answer or just a vote. She wrote a question mark in the margin next to her double underline and left it there, because pretending it was all settled felt worse than admitting it wasn't.

"I still don't get the arrows," Dhruv said. "When you cool it, which way does it go?"

"Towards ammonia. Towards the stuff that makes heat." She drew it again, then drew the factory, a rectangle with little flames under it. "Cold, more ammonia at equilibrium, but slow. Hot, less at equilibrium, but actually happening. Two different questions, and the plant answers both."

"Ms. Morningstar is going to make us explain it out loud," Dhruv groaned. "She'll stand there and wait, like a hawk."

"She gave a whole peroration about partial credit last week," Payton said. "Say the wrong thing confidently and you lose everything. Say the confused thing honestly and you might get half."

Dhruv gathered the pizza box, the phone, his dignity. "Fine. Quiz me on the ammonia thing on the way out."

Payton stood, folded her notes over the question mark so it wouldn't fall out, and followed him to the door while Mario, flat on his back under the minivan, called after them, "When I'm famous, remember this garage. Remember the fries metaphor."

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: In common-law countries such as the US, UK and Canada, a contract generally needs an offer, an acceptance and consideration, meaning something of value given by each side in exchange.
story:
Alexa opened her laptop at the kitchen table and pulled up the website for the summer art program. At the bottom of the registration page, below the fields for her name and her mother's credit card, sat a small grey box: "I have read and agree to the Terms and Conditions." The link beside it went on for eleven printed pages when she clicked it. She skimmed as far as indemnification, saw the word liability for the fourth time, and stopped.

She did not click the box yet. Instead she opened a new tab and typed a message to Melina: did you actually read the terms for this thing or did you just click it. Melina answered a minute later: "clicked obviously. nobody reads those." Then: "why, is something in there?" Alexa didn't know how to answer that, because she didn't know what was in there. She scrolled back to the agreement and read the first section properly this time, moving her finger along the screen the way her mother did with paper contracts.

There was something else nagging at her. Two weeks ago Melia had said, over fries at the food court, that she would pay Alexa twenty dollars a session if Alexa helped her study for the chemistry midterm. They had shaken on it, actually shaken, which had felt at the time like a joke and a promise at the same time. Alexa had done four sessions. Melia had passed the midterm, texted a row of exclamation marks, and had not mentioned the money since. Alexa had not mentioned it either, and the silence was starting to have a shape.

She typed "is a handshake a contract" into the search bar. The results were messier than she expected, forums and a government page and a site that looked like it had been built in 2004. On a plain page from a legal information service she found the sentence she was looking for: in common-law countries such as the US, the UK and Canada, a contract generally needs an offer, an acceptance, and consideration, meaning something of value given by each side in exchange. She read it twice. Something of value given by each side. She had given the tutoring. Melia had offered the twenty dollars. The handshake, she guessed, was the acceptance, though the page did not say what a handshake counted as.

Alexa got up, poured herself the last of the orange juice, and stood at the counter chewing on it. Her mother's voice came from the living room, asking if she was still on that computer. "Homework," Alexa called back, which was not exactly a lie, since she was learning something, though no teacher had assigned it. When she sat back down, she opened a document and started drafting a message to Melia. She wrote "you owe me eighty dollars" and deleted it. She wrote "per our agreement" and deleted that too; it sounded like a lawyer's letter, and Melia would laugh at her, or worse, get stiff.

The back door opened and shut. Mr. Yip from next door was dropping off the mail her mother had asked him to collect, and her mother waved him into the kitchen. Alexa heard them through the doorway talking about the fence quote, and then her mother saying, "Don't sign anything until we see it in writing." Mr. Yip said, sagacious as ever, "In writing is just habit. What matters is offer, acceptance, and consideration." Alexa stopped typing. Her mother asked what that meant, and Mr. Yip said, "Something of value from each side. In common-law countries, anyway. The US, the UK, here." He held up the fence quote. "This is an offer. If I nod and pay half up front, that's acceptance and consideration." He said it lightly, the way he talked about tomato stakes, and then he was out the door again with his canvas bag.

Alexa sat very still. It matched what the webpage had said, word for word almost, and hearing it out loud made it solid. She turned back to her document. It wasn't that she now knew Melia owed her eighty dollars; it was that she knew the thing had a structure, that people had gone to the trouble to codify this exact situation, handshakes and all, into rules old enough that Mr. Yip could recite them while holding a fence quote. But the rules told her what a contract was, not what to do about a friend. Melia had said the words and shaken the hand. Alexa had never said "deal" out loud. Maybe nodding and pulling out the chemistry notes had been her acceptance, or maybe nothing counted between friends, because between friends you weren't supposed to keep score in the first place.

She thought about the grey checkbox still waiting in the other tab. Her mother would sign the art program form without reading it, the way she clicked through everything, and Alexa could either read the eleven pages herself or let it go. She thought about how "shake on it" was a colloquialism her grandfather used, and how the same gesture appeared in those old legal pages, translated into offer and acceptance and consideration, as if the law had taken a phrase from the food court and dressed it in a suit.

She typed a new message to Melia and this time she let it stand. "congrats again on the midterm. also, you said twenty a session and i did four sessions. i'm not mad, i just didn't know if you forgot or if it was a joke when you said it." She looked at the sentence for a long moment, cursor blinking after the period. Then she minimized the document, went back to the art program tab, and started reading the terms from the beginning, her finger tracing line by line, while the message to Melia sat unsent in the corner of the screen. Down the hall, her mother called, "Alexa, did you click agree yet?"

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: India has marked voters' fingers with indelible ink based on silver nitrate since its 1962 general election, so no one can vote twice.
story:
The line outside the middle school gymnasium moved in short, reluctant shuffles, and Nathan stood in it with his registration card going soft in his sweaty hand. His father had texted twice before eight: Don't embarrass me. Vote the whole ticket. Nathan hadn't answered. The second text was a photo of the sample ballot with one name circled so hard the pen had torn through the paper, and Nathan understood it was meant as a map, not a suggestion.

He'd stayed up most of the night with his uncle's photograph open on his laptop instead. His uncle, his mother's brother, lived in Bengaluru, and after the election there he had posted a picture of himself grinning outside a polling station, holding up his index finger like a small flag. The finger was stained a deep violet-black from the knuckle up. When Nathan had asked him about it over video call, months ago, his uncle had been delighted to explain. "Indelible ink," he'd said. "Silver nitrate. We've used it since the 1962 general election. So no one can vote twice." He'd waggled the finger at the camera. Nathan had laughed at the time. Now the gesture seemed almost solemn, a mark you carried out of the station and wore for days, proof that you had done something that could not be undone or repeated.

"That's a long face for a Tuesday," Kacey said. They were in his civics class, though "with" was more accurate; they'd exchanged maybe forty sentences all year, most of them about homework. Today Kacey wore a poll worker's badge on a lanyard and held a clipboard, working the line for anything that might slow it down.

"My dad wants me to vote his whole ticket," Nathan said. "I don't want to vote his ticket."

"So don't."

"It's not that simple. He's not simple." Nathan didn't know how to externalize any of it without it sounding like a complaint, so he stopped trying. "Is the line always like this?"

"Off-year, it moves fast. You'll be inside in ten minutes." Kacey looked at his card, then at his face, and stamped something on the clipboard. "And Nathan, listen. Nobody in that gym sees your ballot. Not the scanner, not me, not the old ladies with the stickers. It's a curtain. What you do behind it is yours."

Nathan got to the check-in table, signed his name next to a printed copy of it, and heard his own voice say thank you too loudly. The booth smelled like disinfectant and somebody's perfume. He pulled the curtain and stood there for a long moment with the ballot flat under his palms.

From the check-in table, Kacey watched the curtain at booth six stay closed long past the usual thirty seconds. An older man in a sectarian party windbreaker, the kind whose loud red lettering had been shouted about all over the local news, coughed pointedly from three places back. Kacey had heard enough of that movement's oratory at the county fair to know exactly what he was waiting for, and took a slow, professional pleasure in checking his name character by character. When Nathan finally emerged, his ballot sealed in its sleeve, he was pale but walking steadily, and he slid it into the scanner without looking at the counter.

"Twenty seconds," Kacey said as Nathan passed, holding out the roll of stickers. "You stood there for four minutes."

"I was deciding."

"Deciding, or copying a circle through paper?" Kacey's voice stayed light, but both of them heard the edge under it.

Nathan peeled a sticker and pressed it onto his jacket, then looked at his own hand, clean and unmarked, flexing it once. "Nobody will know I did this tomorrow," he said. "In India they mark your finger so it shows for days. Silver nitrate, since their 1962 general election, so nobody can vote twice. My uncle holds his up in photos like a trophy." He turned the hand over. "Here you just get a sticker and everyone forgets, including me probably."

"Not the scanner," Kacey said. "It counted you."

Outside, Nathan stood on the curb with his phone in his hand, his father's torn-circle photo still unanswered on the screen. He typed "I voted," then deleted the period and retyped it, and put the phone in his pocket with the screen dark.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: An adjustable-rate mortgage's interest rate changes periodically with a market index, so its monthly payment can rise, unlike a fixed-rate mortgage's.
story:
Nicholas sat at the kitchen table with his laptop open to a rental listing, the cursor blinking over a one-bedroom apartment eight blocks from campus. Fourteen hundred a month, plus a security deposit of one month's rent, refundable if he didn't wreck the place. His mother had said the words "down payment" at dinner in a tone he was still trying to parse, and he'd told her he'd look into it, which was how most of their conversations about money ended: with him alone at a screen.

He opened a calculator and typed his summer wages into it. Then a message popped up from Miah, who had found a room in a shared house for six-fifty, deposit two hundred, and was sending the link before she could lose her nerve. "Take it," he typed back, and meant it, and kept scrolling his own listing anyway, wanting the place that was entirely his even if the arithmetic said it shouldn't be.

The doorbell rang. It was Ms. Taylor from two doors down, holding a plate of lemon bars and looking like she had come for a reason. "Is your mother home?" she asked, and when he said she'd be back at seven, Ms. Taylor set the plate on the counter and stayed. "I'll wait a little," she said. "My mortgage went up. Three hundred dollars a month. I needed to say it out loud to somebody."

Nicholas frowned. "Nothing else changed? The house is the same house."

"The house is the same house." She straightened the fork on the plate. "When we bought it, Rafael's father told me to take the adjustable-rate mortgage. The rate changes every so often with a market index, so the payment can rise. That's what adjustable means, I suppose. He said it was cheaper at the start."

Nicholas pulled his laptop toward him and opened a new tab, keeping one eye on her face, which had gone flat the way his mother's did at the end of a shift. He typed "adjustable rate mortgage payment rise" and read half a paragraph. Fixed-rate, the payment never moved; adjustable, it could. He sat back. "So the bank basically bet against you," he said.

"Or I bet on myself," Ms. Taylor said. "I expected to refinance by now. Then my hours got cut, and my credit got thin, and here I am bringing lemon bars to your mother so I can practice saying it."

He walked her out, and on the porch she pointed at the For Sale sign on the corner lot and said something about the sellers wanting twenty percent down, which was more money than he had earned in his life. After she left, he went back inside and called Rafael, who was at college and answered on the fourth ring with music behind him.

"Your dad does mortgages," Nicholas said.

"He does loans. Close enough. Why."

Nicholas told him about Ms. Taylor, about the three hundred, about how the house hadn't changed and she hadn't missed anything and the payment had still climbed. Rafael was quiet long enough that the music resolved into a new song. "Yeah," Rafael said. "That's the deal she signed. My dad used to call it betting on the future. He took fixed on our place. Says he sleeps better and pays for the sleep."

Nicholas looked at his screen, at the one-bedroom still open in its tab. He thought about the difference between renting, where a deposit was the worst that could happen to him, and owning, where the ground itself could shift under a payment. He had spent the evening thinking of an apartment as freedom; now it also looked like the small end of something whose large end had put that flat look on a neighbor's face. He didn't have a position yet, exactly, only the two of them side by side: Rafael's father sleeping well, Ms. Taylor not.

"What would you do," he asked.

"I'd ask you what you can afford to be wrong about," Rafael said.

Nicholas laughed once, without much in it. He closed the listing, opened the message from Miah, and typed, "Is the room still open?"

knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: On September 17, 1925, when Kahlo was 18, a streetcar crashed into her bus, leaving injuries that caused her pain for the rest of her life.
story:
The art barn at Camp Wren smelled of cedar shavings and turpentine, and on the third Wednesday of July, Mr. Levy propped a print of Frida Kahlo's The Broken Column on the easel and said, "Tell me what you see. Not what you feel. What you see." Samuel sat in the second row between Margaret and Bryson, a notebook open on his knee, and he wrote nails, then crossed it out and wrote nails, many, forming the seam of a replaced corset. The paint was dry oil, the blues desert-hot, and the figure in the middle stood split open like a wall after an earthquake, a stone column where her spine should have been.

"I see a broken Greek column," Bryson said, "which is a symbol, so basically it means her back is ruined."

"She cries, but her face doesn't," Margaret said. "The tears are on the outside like decoration. Like she painted the crying instead of doing it."

Samuel said nothing. He wanted the last word of the session, the one Mr. Levy would remember, and he was beginning to suspect that the painting was less about ruin than about how a person holds ruin still long enough to look at it. But he couldn't say that yet, because Mr. Levy had a rule: every claim had to be fastened to something visible, a colour, a shape, a placement, or it didn't count. Two days earlier Samuel had called a Matisse joyful and Mr. Levy had said, "Joy is a conclusion, not an observation. Reify it. Turn it into something I can point at." Samuel had looked up the word that night in the dining hall dictionary.

"Composition," Samuel said finally. "The horizon cuts her in half behind the waist, but she's facing us, so the landscape is broken and she isn't, or she is and she refuses to look it. The white cloth is the only soft edge in the whole picture. Everything else has an outline."

Mr. Levy tapped the easel twice, his version of applause. "Friday, you each present a full formal analysis. Colour, composition, symbolism. And you will look up one biographical fact and use it as a lens, not a crutch."

That night, in the camp library, a shelf of mismatched donated books, Samuel found a battered catalogue from a Kahlo exhibition. He read it by the window while moths ticked against the screen. On September 17, 1925, when Kahlo was eighteen, a streetcar crashed into her bus, leaving injuries that caused her pain for the rest of her life. He read the sentence three times. Eighteen. He was sixteen and had spent the afternoon complaining about a blister from new hiking boots. The catalogue had a photograph of her before the accident, in a plain dark suit, looking like someone's stern aunt, and Samuel understood suddenly that the nails and the column were not symbols invented out of cleverness; they were a vocabulary built because ordinary vocabulary had failed.

At breakfast he told Margaret and Bryson what he'd found, and he wanted to say it exactly, because the exactness felt like part of the respect. "September 17, 1925," he said. "A streetcar crashed into her bus. She was eighteen. The injuries gave her pain for the rest of her life."

Bryson nodded, chewing. "So the column is her spine. See, I said her back was ruined."

"That's the lazy version," Margaret said. "You're turning her into an answer key."

Samuel agreed with her and also didn't. The trouble was that the fact cut both ways. It made the painting more serious, and at the same time it threatened to reify everything, to flatten colour into symptom and composition into diagnosis, so that no one would ever again look at that white cloth and ask why it was the softest thing in the picture. He had watched Bryson argue about politics all summer with the confidence of a true ideologue, converting every event into proof of something he already believed, and Samuel did not want to do that to a painting. He wanted to hold the two ways of thinking apart, the formal and the biographical, and let them argue in him without either one winning.

Friday came hot and still. Bryson went first and gave a competent, bloodless talk about symbolism as personal code. Margaret went second and did something surprising: she analyzed only the greens, the profligate spread of desert greens that no desert should rightfully contain, and suggested that the unreal green was where the painting kept its hope, or its denial, and that she couldn't decide which, and that the not deciding was the honest part. Then it was Samuel's turn.

He stood in front of the print with his notes, and he set the notes down on the table instead of opening them. He talked about the split body and the unsplit gaze, the hard outlines and the one soft cloth, the horizon doing the breaking while the woman did the standing. Then he said, "She was eighteen when the streetcar hit her bus. September 17, 1925. My age, almost. And I keep wondering whether knowing that helps or whether it makes me stop looking. Whether I see nails, or whether I see a reason for nails and skip the nails entirely." He paused. "The colours still do things the biography can't explain. The green is doing something Margaret can't explain either. I think a good critique holds both and admits what it can't."

Mr. Levy was quiet for a moment, and Samuel braced for the correction. Instead Mr. Levy reached behind the easel and lifted out a second print, one nobody had seen, a later self-portrait, and turned it toward them. In it she stood against a dense blue background, unsmiling, and the same unbreakable gaze. "Analyze this one," Mr. Levy said. "Same rules. You have twenty minutes."

Margaret leaned over and whispered, "The green in this one's darker. Almost black at the edges." Samuel picked his pencil back up.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Malcolm Gladwell's 2008 book Outliers popularized the '10,000-hour rule', though Ericsson later said the quality of practice matters more than any fixed number of hours.
story:
Jaxon's fingers were too wide for the chord. That was the plain problem. The G required a stretch his left hand had never been asked to make, and when he pressed hard enough to stop the buzzing, the notes came out muffled, like a door closing on a conversation. He had borrowed the guitar from the band room's back closet, where Mr. Bui kept instruments nobody played anymore, and he sat with it after school on a folding chair between the timpani and the trombone racks, working the same four changes over and over.

Brenden found him there on the second Tuesday. He stood in the doorway with his trumpet case hanging from one hand and watched for a while before he said anything.

"You started this like three weeks ago."

"Four," Jaxon said, and moved to the C chord, which was worse.

"Four weeks." Brenden set the case on a chair. "You know about the ten thousand hours, right? Malcolm Gladwell's book, Outliers, came out in 2008, my brother read it. Ten thousand hours to get good at anything. You're seventeen. Do the math, man. Even if you started today and never stopped, you'd be ancient."

"Ancient," Jaxon repeated, but his hand kept moving, and the C chord buzzed against his confidence and lost.

Mr. Bui appeared at the door of his office, which was really just a desk behind a partition, and did not say anything. He was a taciturn man who ran the band by gesture more than by instruction, and when he did speak, it was usually to name a thing briefly and then leave. He crossed the room, took the guitar out of Jaxon's hands without asking, and played the four changes himself, slowly, so that the slowness was the lesson. Then he handed it back and went to his desk. Jaxon understood that he had been playing too fast to hear what he was getting wrong, and he also understood that nobody was going to say so out loud.

He did the math anyway that night, on the back of a worksheet. Ten thousand hours divided by three hours a day was a little over nine years, and he would be twenty-six, which was not ancient, though he could see why Brenden thought it portended something grim, a whole youth spent in a practice room for a skill other people started at nine. Brenden had started trumpet in fifth grade. Brenden had never once, as far as Jaxon knew, had to be a beginner in front of anyone.

The next week Judah came in to print sheet music on the band room computer, and overheard Jaxon arguing with the G chord again. "Still on that?" Judah said, and then, more quietly, because Mr. Bui was at his desk, "My cousin read that same Gladwell book and then found out it's not the whole story. The researcher Gladwell got it from, Ericsson, said later that the quality of practice matters more than any fixed number of hours. It's not the number. It's what you do with the hours." Jaxon asked what that meant, and Judah said he didn't know exactly, he wasn't the researcher, and then the printer jammed and the conversation ended there.

But Jaxon kept the sentence the way he kept the guitar, close and awkward. The next afternoon he set his phone timer for twenty minutes and played only the G and the C, four beats each, listening for the buzz the way Mr. Bui had listened, slowing down until he could hear each string separately, and when his fingertips hurt he wrote the time on the worksheet in a column he had started. Quality, he thought, was not a thing you could count, and that bothered him, because a number was at least certain. Either you had ten thousand hours or you didn't. What he had was a column of twenties and a hand that was learning, in its slow animal way, where the frets lived.

He showed Brenden the column on Friday, not as an argument, just slid the paper across the carpet where they sat waiting for the late bus. Brenden looked at it. "That's like four hours total," he said.

"I know."

"So in your version, four good hours beats four hundred bad ones."

"I don't have a version," Jaxon said. "I have a column." He took the paper back and folded it into his pocket, because the bus was coming, and because there was a question he could not answer yet, which was whether he was actually practicing well or just practicing in a way he preferred to believe was well, and he could already tell that no one, not Mr. Bui, not Judah, not the book, was going to answer it for him. The bus doors opened with their long sigh. Brenden picked up his trumpet case and paused, then said, "Show me the G chord," and Jaxon stood on the curb, swung the borrowed guitar off his shoulder, and spread his aching fingers across the strings.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In the CDC's 2021 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, about 1 in 12 US high school students who had dated reported experiencing physical dating violence.
story:
The bleachers were still warm from the afternoon when Emilie found her seat at the forty-yard line. She had planned to arrive early so she could choose where they would sit, and she had, though she had not planned on the wind, which kept lifting the edges of her jacket until she sat on them. Devon had texted that he would meet her at the gate at seven, and at 7:04 she saw him coming up the aluminum steps two at a time, holding two cups of hot chocolate, one of which he handed her without sitting down first.

"You got the good kind," she said. The marshmallows had already begun to dissolve.

"Royce told me what you like." He sat close, closer than the empty bleachers required, and put his arm along the bench behind her shoulders. She decided this was confidence and not something else. The game had not started yet, but the marching band was playing something lugubrious and slow at the far end of the field, and the crowd murmured under it like weather.

He was funny in the way she had hoped, and by the second quarter she had stopped composing her sentences before saying them. When the home team fumbled on their own twenty, Devon grabbed her arm above the elbow and squeezed, and the squeeze crossed some line from enthusiasm into a kind of grip that left the shape of his thumb printed white on her skin. He let go without looking at her. She pulled her sleeve down over the mark and told herself that it was nothing, that she had grown up with two older cousins who wrestled her on every holiday and had long ago inured her to rough hands, and that this was different anyway, that this was excitement, that she was being the kind of girl who made things into problems.

Royce appeared at halftime with popcorn and dropped onto the bench in front of them, turned sideways, knees against the metal. Royce had known Emilie since ninth grade and knew most of what there was to know. He talked to Devon about the defense for two minutes, and then, when Devon stood to get napkins, Royce watched him go and then looked at the sleeve Emilie was still holding down.

"I saw that," Royce said. "On your arm. He grabbed you hard."

"It was the fumble."

"Em." Royce kept his voice level. "We did this unit last spring, in Ms. Whitehead's class. The CDC's 2021 Youth Risk Behavior Survey. About one in twelve US high school students who had dated reported experiencing physical dating violence. One in twelve. I remembered it because it was smaller than I expected and bigger than I wanted."

She wanted to say that a statistic was not a verdict on one Thursday night in October. She wanted to say that Royce had watched thirty seconds of a whole evening, and that metacognition, which Ms. Whitehead had made them practice, meant noticing when you were fitting a story to the evidence instead of the other way around. What she actually said was, "It happened once."

"Once is how the survey counts it," Royce said. "That's the thing. It doesn't wait until it's a pattern to be real to the people who answered."

Devon came back with a fistful of napkins and the third quarter started, and Royce stayed where he was, eating his popcorn in no particular rhythm, not leaving. Emilie found she could not watch the game. She watched Devon's hands instead, the way they moved when he talked, the way one of them came to rest on her knee and stayed there, warm and heavy, and she could not tell, honestly could not tell, whether she minded it or whether Royce had planted the minding in her, and she resented both possibilities equally.

When Devon leaned in during a timeout and asked if she wanted to walk to the concession stand with him, she said yes, because saying no would have required an explanation she did not have. On the way down the steps he took her hand, and his hand was dry and sure, and at the bottom he steered her past the concession line toward the fence by the practice field, where it was quieter, and she let herself be steered and then she stopped walking.

"You grabbed my arm," she said. "Earlier. It actually hurt. I didn't like it."

Devon looked at her for a long moment, the scoreboard light flickering orange across his face. "It was the fumble," he said. "I didn't mean anything by it."

"I know you didn't mean anything by it. I'm telling you it hurt anyway."

He let go of her hand, not abruptly, but fully, both hands into his jacket pockets. Behind them the crowd made its long collective noise, the sound of a play that could have gone either way. Devon glanced back toward the field, then at her, and she could see him deciding something, though she could not see which way the decision ran, and behind the fence the tackle sleds stood in a row under the far lights, angled into the dark like things waiting to be used.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: By the second derivative test, if f'(a) = 0 and f''(a) is negative, the function has a local maximum at x = a.
story:
Madison sat on her grandmother's porch with a textbook open on her knees and a pencil she had sharpened twice, which was, she knew, a way of postponing. The afternoon light came through the maples in patches, and inside the house her grandmother was on the phone with the insurance company, her voice patient and low. Rayne knelt by the porch rail with a can of pale blue paint, working a brush along the wood in long, careful strokes.

"You said you'd help," Rayne said, without turning around.

"I said I'd help after this problem." Madison looked at the page. The function was f of x equals negative x cubed plus six x squared minus nine x plus two, and she had already found the first derivative, three x squared minus twelve x plus nine, and set it equal to zero, and factored, and gotten x equals one and x equals three. Somewhere in there, one of those points was the top of a hill on the graph and the other was the bottom of a valley. She did not know which was which, and when Ms. Zhou had asked yesterday whether she understood, Madison had said yes, which was prevaricating, and she knew it.

Rayne wanted the rail finished before four o'clock, when the grandmother was being driven home from her appointment, because Rayne had promised her a blue rail the last visit and had then gone home without painting anything. Rayne took promises the way other people took exams. She set down the brush and came over, leaving a handprint of blue on the skirt of her shorts.

"So which one is the peak," Rayne said, reading the page upside down.

"That's the problem. I don't know yet."

"Then guess."

"Guessing is what I did on the quiz." Madison had gotten a 71, and Ms. Zhou had written one word in the margin, uncertain, and had not circled it or underlined it, which somehow made it worse. Ms. Zhou never said much; she just left the word there for Madison to walk around for a week.

Madison flipped back in the textbook, past the section she had half read, and found a worked example that did what she had not thought to do. It took the derivative a second time. She sat with that for a moment. If the first derivative told you where the slope was zero, then the derivative of that told you which way the slope itself was turning. Her second derivative came out as six x minus twelve. At x equals one that was negative six, and at x equals three it was positive six.

"By the second derivative test," she said slowly, reading the box at the bottom of the page and then saying it in her own words to make sure she could, "if f prime of a equals zero and f double prime of a is negative, the function has a local maximum at a. So one is the peak. Three is the valley." She checked it against the shape she imagined, the curve rising and then tipping over at one, falling, then bottoming out and climbing again at three, and the picture held together for the first time all week. The graph had been in front of her all along; she had simply never asked the right question of it. What she still did not understand was why a negative second derivative meant curving downward, only that it did, and she wrote that uncertainty in the margin beside Ms. Zhou's word, in smaller letters, so it would be there when she asked about it Monday.

"That took you four minutes," Rayne said. "You sat out here for an hour."

"I was thinking."

"You were staring at that slide rule on the wall in there, is what you were doing." Rayne pointed at the yellow instrument hanging by the door, which had belonged to Madison's grandfather and which the grandmother refused to take down, an anachronistic thing in a house that now had a microwave and a router, kept there like a portrait. "Also, Isabelle texted you twice. Something about the debate team."

Madison read the texts. Isabelle had written a long message about how a boy on the team had switched sides mid-practice and agreed with the coach about everything, and how she called him a sycophant out loud, in the hallway, and now the coach thought Isabelle had said it first. Madison wrote back a short reply, nothing decisive, and put the phone face down on the boards.

"Pick up the other brush," Rayne said. "I have maybe forty minutes of light and a whole bottom rail."

Madison took the second brush from the tray. The blue went on thin at first and she had to go back over it, but by the third board she had the rhythm, long strokes away from her body, the way Rayne did it without seeming to think. Somewhere between the fourth board and the sixth, she understood that the painting and the calculus were not so different, that both were matters of asking which way something was turning before you committed yourself to the stroke. She did not say this out loud. She painted, and the rail turned blue, and inside the house the grandmother was still on the phone, saying, "No, that's not what I told the first person, let me start again."

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: JUnit's assertEquals takes the expected value first and the actual value second, so swapping them gives confusing failure messages.
story:
The basement smelled like dryer sheets and old carpet, and Deven had pushed his dad's weights against the wall to make room for two laptops on the ping pong table. Victoria set her bag down and pulled out the worksheet Mr. Ito had handed back that morning, folded twice, with a red circle around the last problem. "You said you'd show me the class part today," she said. "Not just the variables. The whole thing."

"Private fields first," Deven said, already typing. "Then getters. Mr. Ito keeps saying it's like the class has walls with one door each." He wanted the project finished by Sunday, because the two of them had signed up for the beginner hackathon at the community college and the registration was nonrefundable, and Victoria knew that his real hope was that a finished project would convince his parents the drive out there was worth the gas money. He turned the screen toward her. "Watch. I make the field private so nobody outside can just reach in and change it."

Victoria typed her own version, a class called Book with a private field for the number of pages, and a getter method that returned it. Her fingers were slower than her mind, and she kept reversing the braces, but she noticed something pleasing in the pattern, the way the class kept its data behind a boundary and only answered questions you were allowed to ask. She wondered whether that was a rule about computers or a rule about people, and then decided she was getting ahead of herself.

Then they reached the testing part, and the afternoon turned capricious. The first test passed. The second test failed, and the message on the screen said it expected a number Victoria knew for certain was wrong, one she had never written anywhere. She read it three times. "Why does it think I expected that?" she said. "I expected the right one."

Deven leaned over, chewing the end of a pen cap. "That's so weird. Mine did that yesterday and I just deleted the test." He said it lightly, like a joke about attrition, how half the class had already given up on the unit and he had almost been one of them. But Victoria stared at the line where she had called assertEquals, and she looked at the two numbers sitting there, and she looked at the failure message again, and she turned the whole thing over in her mind the way you turn a key you know fits but haven't found the angle for.

"Wait," she said slowly. "Expected first, then actual. That's the order it wants." She pointed at her own line, where she had put them the other way around, actual first, and the failure message had simply reported what she had told it to expect. She swapped them, ran the test, and it passed, and she sat back with her hands still hovering over the keyboard, not sure whether to feel clever or embarrassed. "I told it the wrong thing and then blamed it for believing me."

Deven laughed, but Riya, who had come down the stairs halfway through with a bag of chips and no announced purpose, had gone quiet in the corner armchair. She had been listening while pretending to look at her phone, and now she said, "That happened to me too. I thought I was just bad at this." There was something in her voice that made Victoria think the chip bag was a cover, that Riya had come down because she wanted to ask if she could join the hackathon team and had lost her nerve at the top of the stairs.

Victoria turned her chair around. "You want to see it? It's actually a decent trick to know." She re-broke her own test on purpose, swapped the values again, and let the confusing message come back up, then fixed it, narrating each line as she went. Riya pulled a chair over from the card table, and for a while the three of them built another class together, a Song class, and argued pleasantly about whether the length in seconds should be private or not. The argument catalyzed something Victoria couldn't quite name, a feeling that the walls in a class were less about secrecy than about trust, about promising that changes would happen in one place where you could watch them.

Riya had written one getter all by herself when she finally said it, casually, eyes still on her screen. "Is there room for a third person on the team, or is that already decided?" Deven looked at Victoria, and Victoria found she was doing arithmetic she hadn't expected, about the drive, about who would sit in the middle seat, about how much Sunday would change with three people instead of two, and about the fact that she genuinely did not know the answer yet.

"We'd have to ask Mr. Ito if the registration can be changed," she said, which was true, and also not an answer. Riya nodded and went back to typing, her getter compiles green on the screen beside them. Victoria saved her file and then, almost without deciding to, opened the hackathon website and let the cursor rest on the team edit button.

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: A simple random sample of about 1,000 people gives a margin of error of roughly plus or minus 3 percentage points for the whole sample's results.
story:
Zoey taped the printout to the whiteboard at the front of the math classroom, where Ms. Xu's second-period students would see it in the morning, then stepped back to look at it the way Victor would. It showed a bar graph: 48 percent of students wanted the school store to stay open through seventh period, 44 percent wanted it closed, 8 percent weren't sure. Below the graph, in the draft headline Victor had sent her at midnight, it said "Majority of Students Favor Late Hours."

"Nine hundred and eighty-seven responses," Victor said from the second row of desks, where he was clicking through photographs on his laptop. "Basically a thousand. That's huge for us. Last year's survey got like two hundred."

Zoey pulled a chair around and sat on it backward, arms folded across the backrest. The room smelled of whiteboard marker and the custodian's lemon floor cleaner, and the radiator under the window ticked as it cooled. Through the half-open door she could hear Avery in the hallway, arguing with someone about layout deadlines, her voice going up the way it did when she was right and knew it.

"Forty-eight to forty-four is four points," Zoey said. "That's not a majority of anything. That's a coin that landed weird."

"It's the biggest number on the page," Victor said. "Readers don't read past the biggest number on the page."

Zoey had spent Sunday afternoon with her grandmother, who watched two news channels at once and shouted at both, and who had a jaundiced view of every statistic that crossed her television. Everything is rigged, her grandmother liked to say, they ask the people they want to ask. Zoey had started to argue with her, then stopped, because she realized she didn't know enough to argue either direction. That night she had looked up what made a poll trustworthy and what didn't, and one fact had stayed with her, plain and stubborn: a simple random sample of about a thousand people gives a margin of error of roughly plus or minus three percentage points for the whole sample's results.

"Here's the thing," she said now. "Our poll is basically a thousand people. Random sample, we pulled names off the whole enrollment list, every grade, nobody chose to be in it. So our margin of error is about plus or minus three points. For the whole poll. That means the forty-eight could really be anywhere from forty-five to fifty-one, and the forty-four could be anywhere from forty-one to forty-seven."

Victor stopped clicking. "So?"

"So they overlap. So it could actually be fifty-one to forty-four the other way, more people against late hours than for them. We don't know. We can't know. And the headline says 'Majority Favors.'"

Avery appeared in the doorway with a thumb drive in her fist and the expression of someone who had been listening through the gap in the door. "Then don't headline the result," she said. "Headline the fight. 'Students Split on Late Store Hours.' Run the graph smaller. People like a split anyway, it means they get to have opinions."

Victor leaned back until his chair creaked. "You're both killing the story. Nobody shares a story about a tie."

"They share stories that are wrong for a day and then get corrected forever," Zoey said. She stood and pulled the tape off the printout, folded the graph in half. "I'm not running 'Majority.' I'm the editor, and that's not a fact yet."

Victor started to expatiate on the decline of print and the attention economy and how every real newsroom in the country led with the number that sold, and Zoey let him run for a while because he was partly right, and she wanted to hear the whole argument before she decided anything. That was the deal she'd made with herself when Ms. Xu handed her the paper last spring: hear the whole argument, then decide, then say why in one sentence. She hadn't always kept it. In the fall she'd run a piece about the cross-country coach's budget that she'd regretted, not because it was wrong but because she'd known it was thin and had printed it anyway because the deadline was Tuesday and the truth was still arriving. The coach had stopped saying hello to her in the corridor. There was a version of editing that treated a close call as good enough, a kind of utilitarianism of the deadline, the greatest good for the greatest number of readers, and she had felt the pull of it and didn't trust herself to feel it dispassionately.

"Okay," Victor said finally. "Your poll, your call. But put the plus-or-minus thing in the article itself, not just my head. People should know why we're calling it a split. Otherwise they'll think we wimped out."

"I will. Three points, either way, that's the honest range." She held up the folded graph. "And I want a line in there saying what we still don't know, which is basically everything under twenty-fifth of a point."

"That's not a sentence," Avery said.

"It will be by deadline."

The radiator ticked again. Avery handed Victor the thumb drive, Victor closed his laptop with the careful click of a concession, and the three of them gathered their bags while the custodian's cart squeaked past the door. In the hallway, Zoey stopped at the announcement board to check the date of the next staff meeting, and found, pinned crooked over the schedule, a flyer that the student council had printed sometime that afternoon: "Over 900 Polled. 48% Want Late Store Hours. Make It Happen, Admin."

Avery read it over her shoulder and exhaled through her teeth. "Well," she said. "Somebody found your poll."

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: Before DNA can be copied, the enzyme helicase unwinds the double helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds that hold the base pairs together.
story:
The waiting room of the Riverside Animal Clinic smelled of disinfectant and wet fur, and Anna had been there for two hours with her biology notes spread across three plastic chairs. Her dog, a fourteen-year-old spaniel named Biscuit, had stopped eating on Thursday, and her mother had driven them over at eight in the morning, which was why Anna was memorizing transcription from a textbook propped against a vending machine. The exam was Monday. Biscuit was behind the double doors now, being X-rayed for what the vet had called a mass, a word that seemed chosen for how little it told you.

Marissa had sent her a photo of the class study group at the library, twelve highlighters and a pizza box, and beneath it: you're missing the fun, loser. Anna typed a reply, deleted it, and typed a shorter one. The truth was that the group had a way of dissolving into argument; Ludovik, who knew the material cold, had a habit of correcting everyone so gently that it stung worse than mockery, and their friend Priya had become his chief detractor, claiming he explained things only to prove he could. Anna liked them both. She just couldn't afford the noise today, in either sense.

Mr. Aquino, the vet, came out at eleven pulling off his gloves, and sat down across from her without being asked, which she took as a bad sign or a good one and couldn't decide which. He said they'd found the mass in the spleen and that surgery on a dog this age was a genuine option, not a condolence. Her mother went to make phone calls at the front desk, and Anna, needing somewhere to put her hands, picked the notes back up.

"What are you studying?" Mr. Aquino asked, not the way adults asked when they were being kind, but the way he'd asked about the dog's appetite, like the answer mattered.

"How DNA gets copied and turned into protein. Transcription and translation. There's an exam Monday and I'm going to fail the helicase part." She said it flatly, because saying it any other way would presage crying, and she had decided she wasn't going to cry in a clinic.

He nodded at the Ziploc bag of manganese treats in her lap, then at her jacket, which was unzipped to the sternum because the waiting room was overheated. "Show me your jacket."

She looked at him. He was old enough to have gray in his eyebrows and a coffee stain shaped like a country on his scrub top, and he waited with the patience of a man who spent his days getting animals to trust him. She tugged the zipper down the rest of the way and laid the jacket flat on the chair between them, the two halves open, the teeth of the zipper gleaming.

"Okay," she said slowly, and then she saw it. "The DNA is the whole jacket. Zipped up, it's the double helix. To copy it, you have to open it first, and the enzyme that does that is helicase. It unwinds the double helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds that hold the base pairs together." She ran a finger along the zipper's track, top to bottom, imagining the little Y of separated strands widening as it went. "Like this. It's an unzipping." It had been a paragraph she'd read eleven times without it meaning anything, and now it was a zipper on a jacket in a vet's office, and she felt the small, almost hedonistic pleasure of a thing finally fitting its slot. "Then each open strand can be read, and RNA gets made off it, and that's transcription, and then the RNA gets read by the ribosome and that's translation, and that's the protein." She heard herself speeding up and slowed down, because Mr. Aquino was still watching, and this was the strange part: he wasn't testing her, he was just listening, and it made her careful.

"Old dog like this," he said, standing, "I'll be back in an hour with the bloodwork. Tell your mother not to decide anything yet." The doors swung shut behind him.

Marissa texted again, a single question mark, and Anna photographed her jacket laid open on the chair, zipper parted down the middle, and sent it with the caption: helicase. Then, before she could decide whether it was wise, she added: study group at the clinic tomorrow? Bring Ludovik, bring Priya, I'll explain this part better than the textbook. Somebody had to hold the strands apart or nothing could be read off them; that much she now understood, though whether Biscuit would come through the surgery, whether she'd pass, whether Priya and Ludovik in one room would be a synthesis or a catastrophe, all of it stayed open. She rezipped the jacket halfway, then left it there, unzipped, on the chair beside her, and turned to watch the doors.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: In Marxist terms, the bourgeoisie owns the means of production, such as factories and land, while the proletariat owns only its labour and must sell it for wages.
story:
Eva had agreed to housesit her grandmother's place for the weekend partly for the quiet and partly for the piano she wasn't allowed to touch at home, and now she was using neither, because she'd spread her English notes across the kitchen table instead. Mr. Adebayo had written one comment at the top of her draft essay on Jane Eyre: "You describe. Now interpret. Try a lens." Underneath, in smaller handwriting, he had added "Marxist or feminist, your choice," as though he were offering her chips.

She texted Maddie, who was technically on a family road trip and replied in fragments between cornfields. "ok so marxist lens = follow the money," came the first message. Then: "who owns stuff vs who works." Eva frowned at her phone. The message sat there like a riddle written by someone who had also not done the reading.

She tried it anyway. On the whiteboard she'd carried up from the basement, a relic of her grandmother's tutoring years, she drew two columns. On the left went the characters who had things: Rochester, with his house and his land and his irritating wardrobe of secrets; Mrs. Fairfax, maybe, though the house was not hers, she only lived in it. On the right went Jane herself, a governess, and Bessie the nurse, and the girls at Lowood who would go out into the world to earn their bread. Eva stood back and looked at the board. The split felt almost too tidy, like sorting laundry into darks and lights and discovering a sock that was somehow both.

The doorbell rang. It was Alaa, helmet under one arm, holding a plastic bag with two mangoes in it, an offering as formal as anything in the novel itself. "Mr. Adebayo told me you were struggling," Alaa said. "He told the whole class, actually. He called it 'a teaching moment.' I hated how he said it."

"He does that thing with his chin," Eva agreed. "Come in. Explain this to me or I'll start eating the furniture."

Alaa circled the whiteboard, tapping the marker against her teeth. "Okay, the words you want are these. The bourgeoisie owns the means of production, like factories and land. The proletariat owns only its labour and has to sell it for wages." She said it quickly, the way you'd recite a locker combination. "My brother drilled me on it for a debate thing. So," and she plucked the marker from Eva's hand, "which side of your board is which?"

Eva looked again. Rochester, column one. He owned land, and the land made money whether he behaved well or profligately, which, given the fire and the bigamy attempt, was mostly the latter. Jane, column two. She owned nothing but her own capacity to teach, to draw, to endure, and she had to sell it, governessing here, teaching at Lowood there, until the inheritance arrived and briefly transfigured her side of the board. "So the whole marriage plot is an economic plot," Eva said slowly. "She can only marry him as an equal once she has money, and she only gets money by accident."

"She gets money by inheritance, which is its own joke," Alaa said. "The system doesn't pay her fairly; a dead uncle does."

Then Maddie's signal returned, and the phone buzzed with a longer message, which Eva read aloud while Alaa peeled a mango with unnecessary ceremony: "feminist lens though: jane keeps saying I have a soul equal to his. like the book knows the marriage is unequal AND fixes it with cash?? is that romantic or is that sad. also is it both. also rochester is profligate lol." Eva laughed, then stopped, because Maddie had landed on the exact knot. The feminist reading said Jane's worth shouldn't depend on money. The Marxist reading said, in that world, it unavoidably did. Bertha Mason, locked in the attic, was the proof of what happened to a woman with no wage and no exit, and Eva hadn't even put her on the board. She picked up the marker and wrote Bertha's name in the margin, belonging to no column at all.

"You look like you've been struck by lightning," Alaa said, mouth full.

"Two lightning bolts. They're arguing." Eva copied the whiteboard into her notebook, columns and margin, and underneath wrote the question she could not yet answer: does Jane's ending count as freedom if it arrives only after the money does? She thought of her grandmother downstairs, forty years of tutoring kids at this table, earning wage by wage the house Eva now sat in rent-free. That was a column too, and Eva was on nobody's board.

Alaa dragged her to the piano before the essay could swallow the whole evening, and they played a duet badly, Eva on the melody, Alaa inventing a harmony that owed nothing to any school of thought. Somewhere in the second verse Eva abandoned the tune entirely, and the two of them hammered out something four-handed and gleeful while the mango pit sat on the whiteboard's ledge like a small trophy.

Later, alone, she opened her draft and typed a new first sentence. Then she deleted it, and typed it again, and left both versions sitting in the document like the sock that was both colors. She underlined nothing. She closed the laptop, went to the window, and watched the streetlight transfigure the garden into a stage set of black paper and gold. "Equal, but with property," she said out loud, to nobody, to the board, and went to bed without deciding.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: Tennessee Williams called The Glass Menagerie, first staged in Chicago in 1944, a memory play: it is narrated by Tom, who looks back on his family.
story:
Jonathan had told everyone the assignment meant nothing to him, which was not entirely true, since he had already written four pages by the time Ms. Owusu asked the class to commandeer the auditorium stage for rehearsal blocks. The unit was a ten-minute play drawn from a moment in the playwright's own life, staged by the playwright, performed by classmates before winter break. He had chosen the night his father's truck disappeared from the driveway, and he had written it as straight realism: a kitchen, a boy doing homework, an engine starting somewhere offstage.

He read it aloud to Emmanuel on the stage, both of them sitting on the edge of the platform with the house lights off and a single work lamp making a yellow square between them. Emmanuel listened all the way through, which for Emmanuel was a form of flattery. When it ended he said, "It's good, but it's a photograph. You're standing outside it."

"I was there," Jonathan said. "That's as inside as it gets."

"Then why do you sound like a court reporter?"

Briar was sprawled in the third row of seats with a copy of The Glass Menagerie on her chest, because she had decided to steal from the best. She held it up without lifting her head. "You should do what he does. Tom steps out and talks to us, and the whole thing is him looking back."

"That's a gimmick," Jonathan said, though he said it too quickly, and then he asked what the play was called, which gave him away entirely.

"A memory play," Briar said. "That's what Tennessee Williams called it. It played in Chicago in 1944, and Tom narrates it, looking back on his family."

Jonathan took the book from her and read the opening stage directions by the work lamp, hunched over, while Emmanuel rehearsed his own scene nearby, playing both a younger brother and a swim coach with alarming volume. The phrase "memory play" sat in Jonathan's mind the way certain words do, refusing to become abstract. It seemed to suggest that a person could stand inside a memory and outside it at once, could admit the whole time that the thing was already over, already lost, and that the telling was its own separate act. It seemed, in fact, to solve his problem, and this annoyed him, because he had liked his problem. It had been a good place to hide.

He rewrote it that night at the kitchen table, and this is the part he would later describe differently, saying the new draft came easily. It did not come easily. He wrote a narrator named Jonathan who steps downstage, addresses the audience, and then steps back into the kitchen scene, and the first three attempts were terrible, either too fancy or too flat, and he deleted them and ate a bowl of cereal at eleven at night out of spite. On the fourth attempt, the narrator said only what the boy in the kitchen could not: that the boy kept doing his homework because as long as the pencil was moving, the night could still turn out some other way. That line was true. He knew it was true because he had to stop writing after it for a while.

At the next rehearsal, Ms. Owusu watched from the fifth row with her coat still on. When the narrator stepped forward, Jonathan, playing his own past self for the time being, watched her face for the verdict. It occurred to him, standing there, that what he really wanted was not for her to like it but for her to believe it, which was a harder and more frightening thing to ask of an audience. She said nothing until the end. Then she said, "Who else has seen this draft?"

"Nobody," Jonathan said.

"Good," she said. "Keep it that way until Friday. You'll be tempted to explain it. Don't."

Emmanuel was cast as the father, which was a joke between them, since Emmanuel was the gentlest person either of them knew and had to practice sounding like a man who leaves. For two afternoons they worked the scene in the auditorium while Briar ran the work lamp, flicking it off and on as the lighting cue for the truck starting. At one point Emmanuel stopped mid-line and said, "I can't do this like a villain. My dad says men like this aren't villains, they're just gone." Jonathan, who had written the father with no lines at all, leaving the engine to speak for him, felt something rearrange itself. He had been certain the silence was honest. Now he was not certain, and he wrote down, in the margin of his script, maybe the father gets one line, and left it as a question.

By dress rehearsal he had made his decision, or rather the play had made it for him. The father got one line, offstage, before the engine: a plain "I'll call," which the audience would know, from the narrator's face, was a lie. It was, Jonathan admitted to Emmanuel, borrowed from real life, though he did not say that the borrow was what made him put off finishing the line for a full day. He had a private theory that everything he wrote about his father was a kind of patrimony, a small inheritance of material he would have traded in a second for the truck to still be in the driveway, and that the theory was probably axiomatic, something he believed without being able to prove, the way you believe a wall is solid until you lean on it.

The night of the performance, the auditorium was full of winter-coat families and the smell of radiator dust. Jonathan stood in the wings with his heart going. He had thought, all week, that he did not care whether anyone came, and now, hearing Briar say her own play's first line out front, he understood that he had been lying to himself about that, and probably about other things too, and that this was not, on balance, a discovery he minded.

The work lamp came up on the kitchen. Jonathan walked out, faced the dark rows of seats, and said, "This is a memory. I'm telling you that now so you'll know how it ends." Then he turned, and picked up the pencil.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Pierre de Coubertin designed the five Olympic rings in 1913, choosing colors so that every national flag of the time contained at least one of them, including the white background.
story:
The screen they'd bolted to the concession stand wall was older than most of the kids on the field, and by the second period it had begun to lean, so the Olympic hockey final played slightly sideways, the rink tilting as though the ice itself were giving up. Hunter sat on the bleacher's third row with his father on one side and Aarav on the other, Milan sprawled across the bench below them shouting at a goalkeeper who could not hear him. The air smelled of cut grass and someone's burnt hot dogs. On his phone, the time read 5:12, which meant he had eighteen minutes before the carpool left for his audition, and he had not yet told his father he was going.

"Again," his father kept saying, whenever the anthem played, whenever the camera cut to the flags hanging over the rink. "Every time, they find a way."

Aarav leaned across Hunter to answer, because Aarav answered everything. "It's a machine for flags. That's all it is. You watch it and it desensitizes you, game by game, until you cheer for a color instead of a person." He said this in the flat, rehearsed way of someone who had said it in class, to Ms. Xu probably, and won the argument there and expected to win it everywhere.

Hunter's father looked at Aarav for a moment, then at Hunter, as if Hunter were responsible for what his friends believed. "Your grandfather watched it on a radio," he said. "No picture at all. He didn't need flags."

"Exactly," Aarav said. "That's the point, that's what it should be."

Hunter didn't answer. He was looking at the rings painted across the screen between whistles, blue, yellow, black, green, red, chasing each other in that sideways loop, and he was thinking about something Ms. Xu had said at the end of their last class before summer, offhand, half a joke: look for your own flag in them, she'd said, and see what you find. His father's flag was saffron, white, green. Aarav's was the same flag. Milan's, from the old country his parents still spoke of with a specific tightness, was red and blue and white, and Milan claimed all three whenever they argued about it.

5:08 now. The whistle blew. Somewhere behind them a small child was crying about a lost glove.

"Pierre de Coubertin designed the rings in 1913," Milan said suddenly from below, phone held up like evidence. "My cousin made me memorize it. He picked the colors so every national flag of the time had at least one of them. Even the white background counts."

"So it was rigged," Aarav said. "From the beginning. Everyone gets a piece of themselves in the picture so everyone stays quiescent and keeps watching. You're literally looking at the mechanism."

"That's one way to see it," Hunter said.

"It's the correct way to see it."

But Hunter was counting on his fingers, low, where his father couldn't watch him do it. Saffron, white, green: the white was there, the green was there. Red and blue for Milan. Blue for half the countries anyone at this field had ever claimed. Every flag on the bleachers folded into that one set of rings, and that could be a trick, Aarav's way, a snare built to catch every nation at once. Or it could be his grandfather's radio, one signal every household could hear and no household turned off. The same five rings, and he couldn't make them be only one thing.

"Time," his father said, without looking at the phone Hunter was checking. He knew the schedule; he'd driven it into the calendar himself, months of auditions and applications, his own project as much as Hunter's. "You should go if you're going."

"I want to see the third period."

"You'll be in a room playing for people who decide things. This is a game on a bad screen."

Hunter stood. The bleacher complained under him. Below, Milan had begun explaining the white background to a woman with the crying child, who had stopped crying to listen, and Aarav had gone back to declaring the whole spectacle a factory for ideologues, gesturing at the crowd as though presenting them to a jury. His father stayed seated, arms crossed, eyes on the tilted rink.

"You'll call me after," his father said. Not a question. Hunter put his hand briefly on his father's shoulder and felt the man not move, not shrug it off either, holding still the way he did when he wanted to say more and had decided he wouldn't.

He walked across the grass toward the parking lot with his jacket over one arm. Behind him the crowd rose all at once, a goal or a penalty, he couldn't tell, and the screen's leaning rings trembled on their white field, still turning.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Mixing paints is subtractive: each pigment absorbs some wavelengths of light, so mixing many pigments together tends toward a dark, muddy color rather than white.
story:
Kaitlyn had wanted the sky in her painting to be a color that did not exist in the tray Mr. Friedman kept locked in the supply closet, the color of late afternoon in November, gold going over to gray. She had a photograph pinned beside her easel, taken from the bus window on the last day of sophomore year, and she had promised Alia the finished canvas by Friday, because Alia was leaving for her grandmother's and wanted something of the studio to take with her.

She started with yellow. Then a thread of blue, then red, then more yellow because the blue had taken over. The palette knife worked the puddle flat and she drew it back toward her. It was brown. Not November brown, not gold-over-to-gray brown, but the brown of a puddle in a parking lot. She scraped it into the trash bucket and started again, and again it went brown, and each time she added something to fix it, the brown got darker, as though the paint were absorbing her intentions along with everything else.

Hugh was two easels down, gluing toothpicks into a bridge that was never going to hold a textbook, let alone the brick Mr. Friedman planned to set on it. He came over when she swore at the tray for the third time. "You're going the wrong way," he said. "You keep adding."

"Because it's wrong. It's too dark, so I add a bright color."

"And then?"

"Then it's darker."

He picked up her knife and turned it over, examining the sedimentary layers of her failures dried along its edge, strata of failed afternoons. "Maybe it's like light," he said. "You know how on the stage crew we learned that all the colored lights together make white? Maybe paint's the opposite. Maybe every color you put in takes something out."

Kaitlyn looked at the photograph, then at the mud on her palette. Each tube on her shelf held a pigment, and every pigment was a kind of appetite, absorbing some part of the light that hit it and handing back only what it refused. Yellow ate the blue wavelengths. Blue ate the red. Pile enough appetites together and nothing survived to be reflected. It was the reason her mixture crawled toward darkness instead of toward white. The colors were not building; they were subtracting.

"Subtractive," she said aloud, testing the word. "That's what it's called. Mixing paint is subtractive."

"That's a terrible name for a color," Hugh said, and went back to his bridge.

Mr. Friedman passed behind her with his coffee and said nothing, which from him was a kind of applause. The studio was in its after-school interregnum, the hour between the children's class and the adult one, when the older students had the room to themselves and the radio played whatever the last person had left it on. Kaitlyn laid out a fresh palette and thought about what the word meant for her plan. She could not build the color by addition. She would have to start close and move carefully, a breath of blue into a generous field of yellow, no more, watching what vanished with each stroke.

Alia arrived early, cheeks cold from the walk, and stood in front of the canvas with her coat still on. "It's not done."

"It's not done," Kaitlyn agreed. The sky she had now was almost right, a thin gold gone slightly to gray at the horizon, and it had cost her four attempts and most of her yellow. "The color you want, you can't get there by wanting more of everything. You get there by taking away less."

"That's very deep for a Tuesday." Alia pulled off her coat. "Can I have it anyway?"

Kaitlyn lifted the canvas off the easel and held it at arm's length. There was a streak near the center where she had panicked and added red, and it had gone almost black, a bruise in the November sky. She could paint it out. She could leave it.
