Hugh's bridge collapsed across the room with a clatter of toothpicks, and Mr. Friedman said something dry about the laws of physics, and Alia was already holding out her hands for the painting, bruise and all.

"Take it," Kaitlyn said, and turned back to the clean palette, squeezing out a small, deliberate field of yellow.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: Hans Krebs and William Johnson described the citric acid cycle in 1937, and Krebs shared the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for it.
story:
Andrew had lost the group somewhere between the pendulum and the glass case of meteorites, which was how he came to be standing alone in front of a wall-sized diagram of a mitochondrion, its inner membrane folded like a curtain blown sideways. The label said THE POWERHOUSE, and beneath it a sequence of arrows carried a glucose molecule through glycolysis, into the matrix, around a circular pathway marked in gold, and out the other side as a disbursement of ATP, thirty-odd coins of energy paid out to the cell. He traced the arrows with his finger, not touching the glass, and felt the strange satisfaction of a map that actually matched the territory he had been staring at in his biology textbook since September.

He was there because Ms. Wilson had assigned it. The worksheet in his jacket pocket had eleven questions, and question nine was the one he had skipped twice: trace the path from glucose to ATP, naming each stage in order. He could recite the words, but reciting felt like claiming a road he had never walked.

Behind him came the squeak of sneakers, and then Clayton, holding his own worksheet like a receipt he intended to argue with. Clayton's plan for the afternoon was public and specific: finish the sheet by two, take the train to the food trucks by the river, and be first in line at the window that sold the dumplings, because last time they had sold out by three. He checked his phone, put it away, and read the wall over Andrew's shoulder.

"Okay, glucose goes in," Clayton said, pencil hovering. "Then this circle thing. What is it, the... Calvin cycle?"

"No, that's plants, that's photosynthesis." Andrew leaned closer. The gold circle was labeled in small type, and he read it aloud. "Citric acid cycle."

"So why do people call it the Krebs cycle?" Clayton's pencil tapped the glass. "Some guy named Krebs, I guess. Why does a body part in a cell have a person's name on it?"

Andrew looked at the small placard beside the diagram, a rectangle of cream-colored card with faded type, half shadowed by the edge of the display case. He had to crouch to read it, one knee on the cool terrazzo floor, close enough to smell the faint dust and lemon of the glass. The card said that Hans Krebs and William Johnson had described the citric acid cycle in 1937, and that Krebs had shared the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for it.

"Because they figured it out," Andrew said. "Krebs and a guy named Johnson described it in 1937. Krebs shared the Nobel for it in 1953."

"Sixteen years later," Clayton said. "Slow payout."

"Careful payout," Andrew said, and surprised himself with the thought that followed, that a discovery like that had to be checked and rechecked, its edges delimited by other people repeating it, before anyone handed over a medal. He stood up. "It's not like he knew it was right that day."

Clayton wrote rapidly, filling in blanks, while Andrew stayed with the diagram. He followed the glucose through glycolysis, watched it split, watched the fragments enter the gold circle and turn, carbons shed one by one, until what remained joined an electron transport chain strung along the folded membrane. He had always thought of the cell as a factory, noisy and mechanical. Standing there, listening to the museum's quiet hum and the distant laugh of some child at the pendulum, he thought instead of a household, careful and frugal, where nothing was wasted and every transaction was recorded. The factory picture and the household picture were both true in their way, and neither was complete; that, he could admit, he still could not reconcile.

"Question ten," Clayton said. "What happens if the cycle stops?" He squinted at the placard, then at his sheet.

Andrew considered. "The cell runs out of ATP. No energy." He chose the word deliberately, testing it. "It would be pretty deleterious."

"It would be dead, Andrew."

"Dead is deleterious," Andrew said, and Clayton laughed, a short bark that echoed off the high ceiling and made a guard glance over, unbothered.

Ms. Wilson appeared at the end of the hall, collecting worksheets, her lanyard swinging. She asked whether question nine had defeated anyone, and Clayton said it had not, waving his sheet, already drifting toward the exit signs and the river beyond them. Andrew wrote out the path one more time in the margin, glucose to pyruvate to the cycle to the membrane to ATP, then folded the sheet and followed.

Outside, the afternoon had gone bright and cold. Clayton was counting the minutes to the train on his fingers. "If we run," he said, "we make the two-fifteen."

Andrew tucked the worksheet deeper into his jacket, against the wind. "Then run."

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: After the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, some Soviet archives became available to researchers, giving historians evidence about Stalin's decisions that earlier writers never had.
story:
The library smelled of old carpet and the lemon cleaner the janitor used after third period, and Anna had spread her materials across two tables pushed together because one was not enough. On the left lay the book by the historian who argued that the Cold War grew from Soviet expansion, Stalin's appetite for control, ideology hardened into policy. On the right lay the book by the historian who argued that the United States had misread insecurity as ambition, that each move the Soviets made was defensive, a hedge against encirclement. Between the two stacks sat her notebook, open to a page headed simply: Evidence?

Calla dropped into the chair opposite and pulled the notebook toward her before Anna could react. "Is this for Mr. Lin's class? He assigned you the archival thing, didn't he." She said it as an accusation, though of what Anna wasn't sure. Calla wanted the topic herself; she had said so twice in seminar, leaning forward, and when Mr. Lin gave it to Anna instead, Calla had laughed in a way that presaged a week of this. "You know I've read all of the revisionist stuff. Twice."

"Then help me," Anna said, and pushed the second book across the table, keeping her hand on the cover a moment longer than necessary, as if letting go of it were a decision.

Calla flipped to the index, which Anna had already marked with torn slips of paper. "So the guy who says Stalin was aggressive, when did he write this?"

"Nineteen sixty-two." Anna found the copyright page and turned it so Calla could see. That was the thing she kept circling back to, the date, more than any argument. The other book was from the nineties. She had noticed it two nights ago at her desk at home, her mother calling her down for dinner twice, and had sat there with her finger on the two dates as though they might reconcile themselves if she stared long enough.

"Okay," Calla said, "so the sixty-two guy didn't know what Stalin was actually doing. He was writing inside the whole zeitgeist, the fear, all of it. The later one had sources." She looked up, waiting to be told she was right.

But Anna had learned, sitting in this library after school for three days running, that it was not that clean. "It's not just that the later one had more confidence," she said slowly, assembling it aloud for the first time. "After the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, some Soviet archives opened up. Researchers got in. The nineties historian is working from Stalin's own decisions, papers nobody in 1962 could touch." She heard the sentence land in her own ears and turned it over. "So when he says Stalin's moves were calculated, he's standing on evidence. And when the earlier one says the same thing, he's standing on inference that happened to point the same direction. Same conclusion, different ground."

"Then what's the problem? Pick the nineties guy." Calla was already reaching for the notebook again, and Anna covered it with her palm.

"The archives aren't everything. Some, not all. And the defensive argument doesn't just evaporate because we can see some of what Stalin decided. Maybe both things are partly true and the evidence we have can't split them." She thought of Mr. Lin, who had said only, "Weigh them against the evidence, Anna, and tell me what survives," and had then declined to say anything further, which she had found infuriating and now found instructive.

Calla leaned back and crossed her arms. "You're going to write that you don't know. He'll think you dodged."

"Or he'll think I read them." Anna wondered, briefly, whether her resistance to Calla's certainty was a real judgment or something extrinsic, a reflex against Calla herself, against the way Calla had claimed the topic as hers. She couldn't fully separate the two, and she let that stand.

The lights above the stacks ticked as the timer began its afternoon countdown to closing. Calla uncapped a pen anyway, spun the notebook toward herself, and drew a line down the middle of a fresh page. "Fine. Left side, what the archives support. Right side, what they don't settle. I'm doing this even if you got the topic."

Anna pulled the second book back across the table and opened it to the appendix. "Start with Stalin, 1945," she said.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Reporters Without Borders' World Press Freedom Index, published since 2002, scores 180 countries and counts concentration of media ownership as one pressure on press freedom.
story:
Sophie had the laptop open on the coffee table and the remote wedged under her thigh, because Kaden kept reaching for it whenever the commercial break dragged. The three of them had colonized her living room after school, textbooks fanned across the rug, her mother's low murmur drifting from the kitchen. On the television, a cable news segment about the proposed closure of the Rowley plant scrolled past beneath a banner that read JOBS OR WASTE.

"That's the third time they've led with the councilwoman's gaffe," Kaden said, pointing at the screen with a pretzel. "The plant thing got forty seconds."

"For your essay, can't you just pick the channel your side already likes?" Hailie was lying flat on the couch, her essay notes balanced on her stomach. "That's what everyone else does."

Sophie didn't answer right away. She had spent the weekend reading two accounts of the Rowley closure that disagreed about nearly everything, and the disagreement had begun to feel less like a mystery and more like a design. The channel was owned by a company whose board included a man whose firm had underwritten the redevelopment proposal for the plant site. She had found that in forty minutes of clicking, which was either investigative instinct or paranoia, and she could not yet tell which.

She typed instead of saying so. Her essay assignment, from Mr. Hussain's class, was to argue a position on whether citizens should trust institutional news, and he had told them, in his dry way, that he would fail any essay that treated trust as a switch instead of a dial. She wanted something firmer than her own suspicion to parametrize the dial with, some way to grade the grading itself, and so she had gone looking for how press freedom was actually measured. That was how she had landed on Reporters Without Borders and their rankings, and it was there, in the methodology section, that she found the sentence that rearranged her evening. The index counted the concentration of media ownership as one of the pressures on press freedom, right alongside the more obvious ones.

"Look at this," she said, and turned the laptop so the other two could see. Hailie sat up, which for Hailie was a major concession.

"It's called the World Press Freedom Index," Sophie said. "It scores a hundred and eighty countries, and they've published it since 2002."

"So where do we rank?" Kaden leaned in, chewing.

Sophie scrolled. Their country sat well up the list, not first, not ruined, somewhere ordinary and arguable. She read the accompanying notes aloud, haltingly, because the vocabulary was denser than her Friday brain wanted. Ownership concentration was not a footnote to the index; it was load-bearing, part of the arithmetic.

"Wait." Hailie pulled her ponytail over one shoulder, thinking. "So it's not just about governments jailing reporters. It's about who owns the paper."

"And the channel," Kaden said, eyes going, without seeming to decide to, to the television.

Sophie sat back on her heels. She was aware of a small, uncomfortable clarity settling over the room, the kind that felt like igneous rock cooling, hard and newly formed. She had wanted to prove the cable channel was lying, and the index had not proven that at all. It had proven only that the question of who pays for the microphone was a recognized, measured, international pressure, not her private conspiracy. The councilwoman might genuinely have flubbed her numbers. The forty seconds might be sloppiness rather than artifice. She could not get from ownership to intent, and she suspected nobody cleanly could, which was either the failure of her essay or its actual thesis.

"Okay," she said slowly, and pulled the laptop back. "Here's my position. I trust the reporter more than the owner, and I check who the owner is before I decide how much." She began typing the sentence, then stopped. "But I can't claim the coverage is biased. Only that it could be, structurally, and that a whole organization exists to watch for exactly that."

"That's not a fun essay," Kaden said.

"It's not supposed to be fun," Hailie said, and stole his pretzel.

From the kitchen, Sophie's mother called that dinner was twenty minutes away, and the segment on the plant came around again, the same banner, the same forty seconds, the same bright smiling anchor. Sophie watched the anchor's face this time instead of the words, and found she could not read anything in it at all.

"Pass me my notes," she said to Hailie, and kept her eyes on the screen.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A metronome marking of 60 means sixty beats per minute, exactly one beat per second.
story:
The auditorium smelled of dust and radiator heat, and Brayden had it to himself until four o'clock, which gave him ninety minutes with the school's baritone saxophone before the jazz ensemble arrived. He had wanted this instrument since September, when Sterling let him hold one for a photograph and the weight of it surprised him, less like an object and more like a commitment. Ms. Oyelaran had signed the practice slip without ceremony, only saying that the room was free until the choir needed it, and that whoever used the piano bench last should put it back.

His problem was a passage eight bars long, marked fast, and it fell apart every time. His fingers knew where to go in theory; his ears told a different story, a smear of notes with one wrong one buried in the middle like a stone in bread. He tried it louder, then softer, then with a kind of aggressive hope, slamming through the smear as though speed might crush the error out of it. The mistake survived every attempt. It seemed almost smug about it.

Sterling came in at three forty with a gym bag and no explanation, sat in the fourth row of seats, and ate a mandarin orange in the loudest possible way. "You're rushing," Sterling said, lobbing the peel toward the aisle and missing. "You rush everything. You rushed the fire drill on Tuesday."

"Fast music is supposed to be fast," Brayden said. The ceiling fans turned slowly overhead, moving the smell of oranges and valve oil around the empty rows.

Sterling came down to the stage, took the metronome from the top of the piano, and wound it. "My cousin does this. She says sixty means sixty beats per minute. Exactly one beat per second." The pendulum began to swing, a wooden click at the bottom of each stroke, patient as a clock in a hallway. "You play it at that. Slow. Slower than you want to."

It felt almost embarrassing, that tick, and Brayden felt the grandiose version of himself shrinking, the one who had imagined performing this piece at the spring showcase with his eyes closed. At one beat per second he had time to think between notes, too much time, and thinking was exactly what he had been avoiding. His fingers arrived early and hovered. His breath ran out because he was holding it. But on the fifth pass, the stone surfaced: the third note of the sixth bar, which he had been hearing as one pitch and fingering as another. It had been hiding inside the smear for two weeks.

He worked the passage at sixty for an hour, until the click stopped being an external thing and he began to internalize it, the tempo moving from the room into his body, his foot keeping time without being asked. When the choir students started drifting in through the side doors with their folders, he pushed the metronome up, then up again, and the passage held. Not perfect. The last bar still tilted. But the stone was gone, and the notes ran connected and clean over the ground where it had been.

Ms. Oyelaran appeared at the back of the auditorium, counting heads for choir, and paused with her hand on the door. "That's better," she called down the aisle. "What changed?"

"Sixty," Brayden said, as though it were a complete sentence.

She nodded slowly, as if he had recited some ancient maxim, and Brayden found that the nod pleased him more than applause would have. "The bench," she reminded him, pointing, and then she was gone into the hallway noise.

Afterward, carrying the case out through the lobby, he turned the evening over without settling it. He still did not know whether the showcase was a real possibility or a thing he had invented about himself, and he could admit that; the line between ambition and delusion was not one he could draw yet. But he knew the passage now, knew it in his hands at any speed, and that was not nothing. Sterling was waiting by the doors, and Brayden lifted the case into the light between them. "Same time tomorrow," he said. "Bring the metronome."

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: The Common European Framework of Reference describes a B2 speaker as able to explain a viewpoint on a topical issue, giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options.
story:
The apartment they had rented in Lyon looked out over a square where the pigeons gathered at seven each evening, and it was there, on the third morning of the trip, that Gabriel spread out his debate notes and admitted to himself that he could not yet do any of it in French. His father wanted the family out sightseeing by ten. Gabriel wanted five uninterrupted minutes in a language he had been studying for two years, five minutes in which he would argue both sides of the question Ms. Pham had assigned before departure: whether the city should ban the public feeding of pigeons. The examiners in September would listen, time him, and place him.

He had assumed the task was beyond his level, a kind of punishment for ambition. In his bag, printed out before the flight, was the course outline from the language school, and that evening, while his parents unpacked groceries and argued amiably about cheese, he found the page and read the small print under the heading for his level. The Common European Framework of Reference describes a B2 speaker as able to explain a viewpoint on a topical issue, giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options. He read it twice. His assignment was not a punishment. It was, almost word for word, the definition of what he was supposed to be able to do.

"It matches," he told Ivy over the hotel wifi, his phone propped against a water glass. "The outline, the framework, the whole thing. Five minutes, a topical issue, pros and cons."

"So it's doable," Ivy said. She was back home, her face lit by a desk lamp, and behind her he could see the summer reading she was ignoring. "That's good news, Gabriel. Why do you look like it isn't?"

"Because now there's no excuse." He turned the phone toward the window, the square, the birds already gathering on the café awnings. "If the framework says I can, and I can't, then that's mine."

The next problem was material. His French was adequate for arguing with his mother about museum queues, but a debate needed evidence, and his dictionary kept offering him words he did not trust. In the square below, an old man was scattering bread with theatrical slowness, and beside the fountain a small municipal sign explained, in dense administrative prose, the city's position on the birds. Gabriel copied out what he could decipher. The sign called them a nuisance. The old man, when Gabriel asked him in careful, slow French whether the birds caused harm, shrugged and used a word Gabriel had to write down phonetically and look up later: parasitism, a life lived at another's expense, the city as host. The old man fed them anyway. "They are only doing what the city taught them," he said, and walked off with his empty paper bag.

That night Gabriel drafted, and the drafting went badly in a way that was new to him. At home he argued like his father, who treated every disagreement as a door to be forced. Here, in the foreign language, forcing was impossible; the sentences were too slow, each one a small negotiation. He had planned to argue for the ban, cleanly, decisively. But the sign and the old man had each given him half of something, and he found himself recalibrate his whole position, writing advantages on one margin and disadvantages on the other like a man hedging bets he had been certain of an hour before. It was slower and less impressive, and it felt, unexpectedly, more honest.

On the fifth evening he performed it for his family in the apartment: five minutes on the ban, delivered to his mother's phone camera so he could watch himself afterward. His voice shook on the subjunctives. Twice he stalled and restarted. But he gave the advantages, the cleaner facades and the smaller flocks, and the disadvantages, the feeders driven to secrecy, the birds simply relocated to some other district's statues, and then he said the thing he had not planned to say, that he did not know whether a city could be a host that also chose its guests, and that maybe the question was not whether to ban the feeding but whether anyone had ever asked why the feeding began. His father, who had wanted his son to spend the trip becoming fluent for reasons that were frankly extrinsic, a line on an application, a ranking, stopped checking his email somewhere in the third minute.

Afterward Gabriel watched the recording once, wincing, then set the phone face down. Ivy had messaged: did you do it. He typed that he had done it badly and truthfully, and that he no longer knew which of those mattered more for September, or whether the examiners would reward a man who changed his mind halfway through a debate or fail him for it.

In the morning the square was quiet, the café chairs stacked, the fountain running its thin silver thread. The old man was not there. A city worker in an orange vest swept the crumbs from the pavement into a long-handled pan, methodically, square by square, and Gabriel stood at the window with his coffee until the worker reached the fountain and stopped, looked up at the birds on the awning, and swept around them.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: The 26th Amendment, which set the US voting age at 18, was ratified in 1971 in about three months, faster than any other amendment.
story:
Tyler set his phone face down beside his plate, which was the family rule, though his mother mostly enforced it against his stepbrother and hardly ever against him. The meatloaf steamed. His grandfather was telling a story about 1971 again, or starting to, the way he did whenever an election year came around, and Tyler braced for the part about the draft, which he had heard four times.

"I was twenty when I finally voted," his grandfather was saying. "You'll be able to do it at eighteen. That still surprises me, you know. I couldn't. Nobody could at eighteen when I was a boy."

Tyler picked up his fork and put it down. "Wait. You couldn't vote at eighteen? Like, legally?"

"Legally, spiritually, any way you like." His grandfather laughed, but Tyler was already reaching for his phone, and nobody stopped him, because it was that kind of question, the kind his mother called his law-school questions.

The search took eleven seconds. The Twenty-sixth Amendment set the voting age at eighteen, and it was ratified in 1971, and it had gone from proposal to law in about three months, faster than any other amendment. He read the sentence twice under the table. Three months. His school had spent longer arguing about vending machines.

"Three months," he said out loud, and everyone looked at him. "The whole country changed its mind about who counts in about three months. The Twenty-sixth Amendment. It went through faster than anything else ever has."

"Fastest one on the books," his grandfather said, pointing his fork like a conductor. "I remember the summer it happened. Everyone my age suddenly mattered."

Tyler put the phone down flat on the tablecloth, breaking his own rule, and nobody mentioned it. Here was the thing he could not stop turning over: his grandfather had been eighteen and voiceless, and now Tyler was sixteen, and in what felt like no time at all he would be eighteen and counted. He had assumed voting was something that arrived with a driver's license, automatic as gravity. Apparently it had been fought for, quickly, urgently, by people who thought eighteen-year-olds were adults in every way that mattered except the one at the ballot box.

"Is that why you registered the day you could?" Tyler asked.

"The day after," his grandfather said. "I had to walk two miles to the courthouse. In the rain, if you want the whole legend."

"You do the rain every time," his mother said, passing the green beans.

That night Tyler sat at the same table after dinner, long after the dishes were stacked, with his laptop open to the state election site. In his state you could pre-register at sixteen, and the first actual ballot would come to him at eighteen, two Novembers away. It felt strange to be a neophyte about something that had been his grandfather's whole coming-of-age. He texted Makai, who had mentioned in government class that he thought voting was basically pointless, one drop in an ocean.

"If a million drops think they're one drop, the ocean stays dry," Tyler typed, then deleted it because it sounded like a poster. Instead he wrote, "You know you couldn't have voted at 18 until 1971? Like your dad couldn't have." Makai replied with three thinking emojis and then, a full minute later, "fr?" which Tyler took as a small victory.

The next day Ms. Nikolaidis had them do a debate about mandatory voting, and Chanel argued the affirmative with what Tyler privately considered a specious comparison to jury duty, since juries decide one case while elections set years of policy. He said so, more politely than that, and Chanel came back with the point that turnout itself signals legitimacy, and by the end of the period he had conceded that she was partly right, that the symbolism was a real good even if the logic was shaky. He had gone into the debate sure and came out distributed between two positions, which bothered him less than he expected.

When he told his grandfather he had pre-registered, printed the confirmation and everything, the old man asked to see the page. He read it slowly, moving his lips a little.

"Two years till it counts," he said.

"Two years," Tyler said. "And I still don't know who I'd vote for. I keep changing my mind."

"Good," his grandfather said, and slid the page back across the table. "The ones who never do scare me."

Tyler folded the confirmation in half and put it in the front pocket of his binder, where he could find it again in November of his eighteenth year, and went to help his mother with the dishes.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: Peak bone mass is typically reached in the early twenties in women and the late twenties in men, so bone built in the teenage years affects bone strength for life.
story:
Xavier had been sitting outside the guidance counsellor's office for eleven minutes when the door finally opened and a girl he half knew, Iris, came out wiping her eyes with the heel of her hand. She looked at him, then at the schedule change form folded in his fist, and said, "Don't do it for the wrong reason." Before he could ask which reason was the wrong one, she was gone down the hallway, and Ms. Somsak was saying, "Xavier, come in."

He put the form on her desk between the spider plant and a mug that read WORLD'S MOST ADEQUATE COUNSELLOR. The form asked to drop varsity soccer so he could take the early shift at the warehouse four nights a week. His father had done the math at the kitchen table, tapping the calculator like it owed him something. Out-of-state tuition minus scholarships minus what they had. The gap was the size of a used car, except you couldn't drive a gap to Ohio.

"Tell me what soccer costs you," Ms. Somsak said, which was a strange way to put it, and it destabilized the whole speech he had rehearsed in the parking lot, the one about sacrifices and adulthood. He had expected her to argue about transcripts. Instead she turned her monitor toward him and showed him a spreadsheet of alumni, rows of names and numbers, what past seniors had paid and earned and still owed at twenty-five. "It's not a verdict," she said. "It's just that four years is not the whole picture."

"My grandmother says the same kind of thing," he said. "About bones."

Ms. Somsak raised an eyebrow, so he told her. His grandmother had fallen in March, a hip fracture, and she now did her exercises with a rubber band while the television shouted game shows. When he'd visited Sunday, she'd gripped his wrist and said, "You're still building, you know. Peak bone mass comes in the early twenties for women, the late twenties for men, so what you build now is what you carry your whole life. I sat in chairs when I was your age. I wish someone had told me the chair was a decision." Then she had made him promise to keep lifting the dumbbells in the garage, which he had, so far, only sort of done.

Ms. Somsak wrote something on a legal pad and turned it around: not the words, just a rough timeline with a stick figure at eighteen and a question mark at seventy. "Is your grandmother doctrinaire about this? Mine was about butter."

"She's doctrinaire about chairs," Xavier said, and surprised himself by laughing. "But she's probably right."

The word "probably" sat there. That was the trouble with his grandmother's speech, with the spreadsheet, with Iris and her tear-streaked verdict in the hallway: they were all describing futures he couldn't inspect. He understood, in some new way that he couldn't have explained at breakfast, that every decision was a bet placed for a person he hadn't met yet, a seventy-year-old Xavier, a twenty-five-year-old Xavier, one with strong hips and one without debt or maybe one with both or neither. He said some version of this out loud, badly, and Ms. Somsak did not correct his grammar.

What she did was pick up the form, take out her pen, and draw one line through the word "soccer," then write above it, in small letters, "modified schedule, three practices, Sat. shift only." She slid it back. "The warehouse takes Saturday workers. Your coach took my daughter's schedule apart once for less." She looked at him over her glasses. "You can carry the debt question and the bone question at the same time. They're not actually in competition. You just liked the drama of choosing one."

He took the form. In the doorway he nearly collided with Patience, his teammate, who was there for some crisis with a scholarship essay, and who said, "If you quit I have no one to blame the Tuesday losses on." He told her the modified schedule instead, and Patience punched his shoulder and called him a part-time coward, which from her was affection. Walking out through the double doors into the October light, he read the form again, folded it once along Ms. Somsak's line, and put it in his back pocket where he would feel it every time he sat down.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The 2026 FIFA World Cup, hosted by Canada, Mexico and the United States, was the first with 48 teams and the first hosted by three countries.
story:
Lea arrived at the community field early enough to claim the patch of grass at the top of the slope, where the portable screen had been staked between the soccer nets. The town had rigged up a broadcast of the final for anyone who couldn't get to the watch parties downtown, and by the time Holly and Faith spread their blanket beside her, the slope had filled with folding chairs and strollers and a smell of sunscreen and grilled onions. Her mother unfolded a canvas chair a few feet behind her and said nothing, which Lea had learned to read as its own kind of speech.

"Forty-eight," Holly was saying to Faith, who had pulled up something on her phone and was squinting at it. "I'm telling you, it's forty-eight this time. My cousin wouldn't shut up about it."

"Thirty-two," Faith said. "It's been thirty-two since forever."

"It changed. It's the first one with forty-eight teams. And it's not even in one country, it's Canada, Mexico and the United States all hosting it together. Three countries. My cousin printed out the whole schedule." Holly held out her own phone as evidence, and Faith leaned over Lea's knees to look, and for a while the two of them argued the way they argued about everything, less to win than to keep a thread of sound going between them.

Lea let it drift past her. She had played on this field since she was nine, and the grass held a sedimentary record of her whole childhood: the layer of Saturday clinics, the layer of the year she made travel, the thin layer of last spring, when she'd told the coach she needed to focus on applications and walked off before he could answer. Her mother had called it a sensible decision, and had repeated the word sensible so often that it began to delimit Lea's entire future, a fence drawn around what she was allowed to want. What her mother never said, and what Lea never said either, was that the applications had taken four weekends total and the rest of the season had gone to watching other people play.

A memory came to her without being invited. She was eleven, maybe twelve, riding home from a rainout with Mr. Katz, whose house backed onto the field and who had driven half the team home for years. She had been crying about a missed penalty, and instead of consoling her he had told her about a tryout he'd skipped at her age because his father said sport was a dead end. "I still don't know if he was right," Mr. Katz had said, hands loose on the wheel. "That's the part nobody tells you. You find out which choices were right about forty years too late." She had thought it was a strange thing to say to a child. Now it felt less strange.

On the screen the teams walked out of the tunnel into a wall of noise, and the crowd on the slope answered it, a hundred strangers roaring at once. Faith finally looked up from her phone. "Okay. Forty-eight. First time. Three countries. Holly's cousin wins."

"Three countries," Holly said, settling back with the satisfaction of a lawyer resting her case. "Canada, Mexico, the United States. First time for that too."

Lea found herself watching her mother rather than the match. Her mother was holding a paper plate of nachos she wasn't eating, and when the camera swept across the flags in the stands, her expression did something small and unreadable. Lea thought about walking over. She thought about what she would say, which was nothing rehearsed, only that she'd quit for reasons that had felt solid at the time and felt porous now, that every adult who'd ever weighed in, her mother with her pragmatism and Mr. Katz with his shrug, had offered a way of thinking about it, and neither way had actually told her what she wanted. She could hold both of them, she understood suddenly, the way the tournament held three countries; that didn't mean the thing held together was coherent. It only meant it was happening.

At halftime she did stand up, brushing grass from her jeans. Faith asked where she was going and Lea said, "Down to the fence," which was true but not the whole truth, because the fence was where Mr. Katz stood every game he attended, elbows on the rail, watching the empty practice field the way other people watched the screen. The slope was a morass of blankets and coolers and she picked her way through it, and when she reached him he glanced over without surprise, as if he'd been expecting her for about forty years. "Halftime already," he said.

Lea put her elbows on the rail beside him. "I wanted to ask you something about when you quit."

"Ask," he said, and turned back toward the field.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During Japan's Buddhist festival of Obon, families light fires to welcome the spirits of ancestors home, and at the end many float lanterns down rivers to guide the spirits back.
story:
Aaron had not wanted to come inside the house. He stood in his grandmother's backyard instead, holding the screen door half open, until she noticed him through the window and waved him in with a spatula. The kitchen smelled like the miso his grandfather used to make on Sundays, and the wrongness of that, the pot on the stove with no one to complain it was too salty, made Aaron's throat close. His grandfather had been dead for eleven days. The doctor had used the word etiology in the hallway outside the hospital room, saying the cause of the heart failure was unclear, and Aaron had looked the word up in the parking lot because he needed something to do with his hands.

"You're just in time," his grandmother said, as if he were late for dinner and not three days late for the funeral arrangements. On the table lay a stack of paper lanterns, flat and square, and a box of markers. "Sit."

He sat. Through the window he could see the small iron bowl she had set by the back step, already stacked with kindling. When he asked what it was for, she only said, "Obon. We light fires so the spirits can find their way home." She said it the way she said everything, brisk and certain, and turned back to the stove before he could ask which spirits, or whose.

He texted Gemma from the bathroom because he did not know who else to text. My grandma's doing some festival thing. For him, I think. Gemma replied with a thumbs up and then, thirty seconds later, sorry that sounded nonchalant, I don't know what to say either. Aaron read it twice. He had been trying all summer to contextualize the loss, to fit it into some framework that would hold, telling himself his grandfather was eighty-one, telling himself it was quick, telling himself everyone dies. None of it worked. It was like trying to file a document in a cabinet that had no drawer for it.

Back at the table, his grandmother pushed a lantern toward him. "Write his name," she said. "And something you want to say." Aaron's marker hovered. He wrote his grandfather's name in careful katakana, the characters his grandfather had drilled into him two summers ago, sitting at this same table with a workbook and a fan. Then, underneath, he wrote in English: I should have called more. He did not show her.

At dusk she lit the fire in the iron bowl, and they stood side by side while it burned down. Aaron kept expecting to feel something arrive, some presence moving through the smoke toward the house, and felt instead the specific embarrassment of a seventeen-year-old standing in a backyard performing a ritual he did not fully own. He almost said so. He almost said, I don't know if I believe this. But his grandmother's face in the firelight was not performing anything. Her jaw was set the way it had been at the funeral, and he understood that the question of whether the spirits were real was not the question she was answering. She was answering a different one: what do you do with your hands.

The next evening they drove to the river, because, as his grandmother explained to the woman parking cars, tonight was the last night, when families float lanterns down the river to guide the spirits back. The water was already crowded with small lights, dozens of them, drifting slow in the current, and along the bank families crouched at the waterline. A boy about Aaron's age launched one and watched it go with his fists on his knees. Nobody spoke much. The whole event had the feeling of a held breath.

Aaron knelt in the mud and set his grandfather's lantern on the water, and the current took it faster than he expected, so that he had to scramble a few steps along the bank to keep it in sight. It joined the others, one light among many, indistinguishable almost immediately, and he kept watching the place where he thought it was even after he could not tell it apart from the rest.

"Say goodbye," his grandmother said behind him, not unkindly.

"I'm trying," Aaron said. The lantern he thought was his, or one like it, caught on a branch near the far bank, hung there, then slipped free and kept going. He stayed until his grandmother touched his shoulder, and then he said it, quietly, to the water: "Okay. Bye, Jiichan." His grandmother took his arm, and they walked back up the bank together, past all the families still crouched at the edge, releasing their lights.
